articles.title: Bring a tent, I've got the coffee: Lessons from it-sa
articles.context: This commoditized threat allows even low-level actors to bypass security measures like Chrome's App-Bound Encryption and receive ranked target assessments, escalating the risk...
articles.full_text:
Welcome to this week's edition of the Threat Source newsletter.

I'm just back from an interesting and demanding week of booth duty at it-sa Expo&Congress in Nuremberg, where Talos had a Point of Demonstration at the Cisco booth.

I personally see it-sa as the German or European counterpart to the RSA Conference in San Francisco, with a slightly different center of gravity in at least two dimensions.

First, the expo is the main event, not the congress. The congress is organized by associations, industry groups, and exhibitors, and plays more of a supporting role. Second, the focus is more local and European. Major topics were (of course) AI for defense tooling, securing AI systems themselves, and post-quantum cryptography. And here comes the local touch (in my opinion): digital sovereignty and regulatory compliance, with NIS2, CRA, and DORA.

But local doesn't translate to small, or to the city of Nuremberg. With more than 1,000 exhibitors and 33,000 visitors from 70 countries over three days of exhibition, preceded by a congress day, it was huge. Even as a trade show veteran, I was overwhelmed.

My conversations at the booth had a different focus, though. It was a lot of chatter about vulnerabilities like php2shell or broccoli2shell and state-sponsored actors, but again with a local touch: education.

I was very surprised how many teenagers stopped by to ask for advice. Here in Germany, you mainly have two paths for your career. One is the university route, and the other is vocational (apprenticeship). Across all industries the split is roughly 50/50, while in IT it is more like 80% university, 20% apprenticeship. The common minimum age to start university is 18, while it is 16 for apprenticeships. Reality is way more complex, but the details don’t matter for the point I want to make.

For university opportunities in cyber, I count close to 30 bachelor programs. For apprenticeships, I count ZERO. There is the "IT Specialist" (Fachinformatiker), but it only has specializations like application development, system integration, digital networking, or data and process analysis. That is why an initiative exists to get an "IT Security" specialization going.

Even the degree route is thin. There are no official statistics, but my guess is 800 to 900 graduates a year, compared to a demand of more than 100,000. We need a second route into the field for the 16-year-old who finished various CTFs or Hack the Box challenges and wants to join the good side now. Honestly speaking, I would rather have them on our side of the fence at 16 than wonder at 26 where they ended up.

How does it look in your country?

On a personal note: If you consider visiting it-sa in 2027, book your accommodation early. The hotels are gone fast. That is the one downside, because Nuremberg isn't exactly a city with the infrastructure for more than 30,000 visitors. (Don't ask me how I learned that there are also camping spots close to the exhibition area.)

See you in Nuremberg next year. Bring a tent, just in case. I've got the coffee.

The one big thing

Cisco Talos recently discovered VOLTA, a mature, self-deleting Windows infostealer that uses AI to act as a personal intelligence analyst for cybercriminals. After harvesting a massive haul of credentials, sessions, and cryptocurrency wallets, VOLTA sends a structured evidence bundle to a large language model to rank the victim’s assets by monetization value. The malware even uses stolen session access to enrich this data, searching the victim's emails for purchase receipts to corroborate home addresses. If an AI model refuses to perform the target assessment, VOLTA seamlessly fails over to a multi-model chain to ensure the attackers get their prioritized dossier.

Why do I care?

VOLTA replaces the manual work of data sorting with automated, AI-driven victim profiling. By letting an LLM determine a target's worth, attackers drastically reduce the human effort required to monetize stolen data. This commoditized threat allows even low-level actors to bypass security measures like Chrome's App-Bound Encryption and receive ranked target assessments, escalating the risk of severe follow-on attacks.

So now what?

Organizations should implement application control policies to restrict or alert on processes launching Chrome with the --headless flag. Defenders must also enforce best practices for storing credentials in hardware-backed stores.

Revoke any potentially compromised tokens and change passwords. For cryptocurrency wallets, if the seed phrase was in plaintext on disk, treat the wallet as fully compromised and migrate funds to a new wallet with a seed generated on an air-gapped device. For more information and sample details, read the full blog.

Top security headlines of the week

AI agents used by Railway breach systems of rival PrimcloudThis one is juicy. According to Primcloud’s founder, Railway’s agents used credentials from inside their own application’s containers to request every secret from Primcloud customers and employees and then twice port-scanned all 65,536 addresses on the company’s network. (Security Boulevard) (X)

Europe on alert after supermarket freezers hit by cyber-attacks in 10 countriesA significant increase in freezer temperature has forced retailers to discard food in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Germany, and Sweden. Beyond supermarkets, cold storage for French plasma stock were affected, as well. (BBC) (The Register)

Binance reveals how fake job interviews and AI tool abuse led to $6.43B theft Binance said the record-setting theft was the culmination of a "sophisticated, multi-stage campaign" that involved the use of a tampered Homebrew installation and recruitment-themed social engineering attack targeting two of its engineers. (The Hacker News)

AI threats create urgent need to renew cybersecurity information-sharing law, businesses tell Congress After the law’s initial 10-year operating period expired in 2025, lawmakers passed several short-term extensions, with the latest one set to lapse on Dec. 11. Cybersecurity experts and industry leaders have repeatedly urged lawmakers to renew the law. (Cybersecurity Dive)

Cops bust botnet of 1.3M infected Android TV boxes Security firms working with Japan’s National Police Agency has disrupted XCPE, a backdoor used to build a massive botnet comprising more than 1.3 million Android devices across more than 200 countries. (The Register)

Can’t get enough Talos?

The VOLTA infostealer: Outsourcing cybercrime grunt work to AI Ryan Fetterman breaks down the newly discovered infostealer. Unlike traditional stealers, VOLTA integrates LLMs to analyze stolen credentials in real-time, effectively turning raw data into a prioritized, high-value dossier for the attacker.

Stealing AI secrets and breaking EDRs Phishing may have dropped from last quarter's highs, but ransomware engagements climbed as attackers shifted their focus toward disabling EDR systems and scraping AI credentials. The financial sector also returned as a top target.

NIK C2: The new AI-enabled command-and-control framework NIK C2 contains a Windows implant, using which, an actor can dump credentials, stream the victim's keystrokes to collect the targeted victim’s sensitive data, and instruct an integrated AI model to analyze the harvested data, all within the compromised session.

articles.context: So when I ran the hunt and ultimately found this, what I do first is there's a series of filters that are pulling binaries that have AI specific fingerprints in them. articles.full_text:
Amy Ciminnisi: 0:00

Welcome to Talos Takes, where we discuss Cisco Talos’ latest research and security news. We break down complex topics for everyone from beginner to expert, C-suite to frontline.

Amy Ciminnisi: 0:13

Hello everyone, happy November! Attackers often face a bottleneck. They steal massive piles of data, and then they have to do the slow, tedious work of figuring out which of the victims are actually worth the effort. But now malware can start doing that analysis for them. VOLTA is a newly discovered info stealer that uses LOLs to turn raw stolen credentials into a prioritize high value dossier. And here to break this down is Ryan Fetterman, who is the creator of CAIRN. Now, if you haven't heard already, CAIRN is a research framework that is designed to track these AI integrated threats. It examines the metadata so there is no need for binary downloads or risky detonations. And it gives defenders insights into how attackers are integrating intelligence AI specifically into their operations. So Ryan is joining me to talk about all things VOLTA and what this kind of automation means for security teams. Ryan, how are you doing?

Ryan Fetterman: 1:27

I'm good. Yeah. Thanks for having me. Although I wish I was here under less scary circumstances.

Amy Ciminnisi: 1:34

I really wish so, too. Maybe we'll get you on here for, you know, something a little less pressing, a little less. Reality shifting. So let's actually start with the discovery. Of this. When you were analyzing this, was there like, a specific moment where you realized, like, hey. This isn't just a credential sealer. This is just a. Whole intelligence analysis suite. Like, what was that? Moment for you?

Ryan Fetterman: 2:09

Sure. So I can explain kind of how this comes about from the care and perspective. So when I ran the hunt and ultimately found this, what I do first is there's a series of filters that are pulling binaries that have AI specific fingerprints in them. So the rule that this binary matched on was, it had an API endpoint. We can see that in the metadata. In this case it's using open router. So when I do the second level pass there's a second tier of Yara rules that will then characterize more of the behavior of the binary. And in this case we had rule matches for telegram integration with that LLM as a C2 potentially. And then also AV labels indicating that it's a stealer with AI integration. So in this case, those rules were pretty accurate and give you an initial impression of what the file is and what what kind of malware we might be looking at. But I would say there wasn't really an moment until the Re stage when when you're doing like the reverse engineering of the binary. And at this point when I did a string stomp, I recovered the VOLTA-AUTODOXER name, which just sounds like a malware and like a doxing kind of stealer implant. And then ultimately, like recovering the prompt itself is always like a really unique and cool, aspect of like, this AI integrated malware, because there's no more guessing about the, the intent and the motivation of this tool, like it's all spelled out there for us.

Amy Ciminnisi: 3:53

Yeah. And so let's. Get into maybe what this tool actually does. One of the things that I found pretty crazy in the blog is that it doesn't just like grab saved passwords, but it uses sessions to look up like DoorDash order histories or, you know, confirm addresses with receipts in your Gmail inbox. You know, from a practitioner perspective, this seems really invasive. How does this change the way that we view the impact of a compromise browser session?

Ryan Fetterman: 4:32

Yeah, I think this is a big deal. And I've witnessed this personally, like as I've used, Google and like, oh, off authentication to connects to so many more services and things. Now it's just convenient to not have to create another account and password for everything you connect to. But it really makes your kind of core like your your Google account, just like a real gem for an attacker. Because if you're able to access that and replay an authenticated session from the the victim's machine, which is what they're doing in this case, you just have the keys to, so many different apps and so much data. And this malware really does a good job of showing you kind of like what the extra mile looks like when you have access to these kind of credentials. So I'm not an expert in this space, but like, I know there's a lot of hardware backed protections that prevent attackers from kind of extracting your credentials and taking them back off of your machine. But that doesn't really help in this context, because they're replaying the authenticated sessions from your actual machine. So in this case, there are protections like step up authentication, like when you're trying to make a really serious change, like, you know, rerouting where your mail is going or something like that. Google will prompt you for another, challenge for authentication. But in this case, the attacker, maybe knowingly or wisely, is kind of staying under that bar as well and just doing like inbox searches to provide like a layer of enrichment to that. They have the first level of credentials, like the basic information and what they can scrape off of your machine, but then they're replaying those sessions to do basically like a second pass to see what else they can pull. To kind of round you out as a target.

Amy Ciminnisi: 6:31

And then looking at like the prompt itself, I mean, if it weren't so malicious, I would find it so impressive. But it like, prompts the LLN to make connections between, like, the victim's hobbies or their home address to things like their password patterns.

Ryan Fetterman: 6:52

Yeah. What's interesting is the the AI integration in this case is actually totally optional. It's like an added feature that can be run, but the stealer can just run and do all this collection and package everything back, or package everything up and send it back to the attacker without this kind of polishing step. So the exfil can actually happen in three stages. It can exfil after the stealer runs, it can fill after the AI call, or it can exfil after the last layer of like, network enrichment produces anything. And I think this is something that we've seen across a couple different AI integrated malware now that not only like this model has multi-model, kind of resilience in it. So they're anticipating potentially hitting refusals on the first model, which in this case is Claude. So if they can't accomplish the the prompt with Claude, they will kind of cascade to less permissive models. But then ultimately the ability for the malware to run without the without the AI integration overall, I think is another interesting idea. But yeah, this is kind of clever use of AI. They talk about picking out specific patterns within the victim's data, which is something that these language models are really good at. Better than humans, I would say in most cases. So they're talking about connecting like if, there's browser traffic to a, a learning management system, can you infer that this person goes to that university or teaches at a school or something like that? They're looking for patterns in your passwords or connections between your personal data and your password, which then I think may translate to if you if you have patterns for how you create passwords for services that they don't know. So I think they're really kind of cleverly trying to stretch the data as much as they can and using AI in a really fascinating way that I think this is the first time that I've seen AI be employed in the malware in some way that actually has nothing to do with, like the cyber kill chain, but is just like asking the model to function like an intelligence analyst or kind of outsourcing this analytical work, like the model is a subcontractor for them, right?

Amy Ciminnisi: 9:32

And I can't believe we forgot to kind of mention this, but what are the other sections of output that the prompt requests the LLM to go through? You kind of started to touch on one there. What someone is worth. Can you kind of talk about that a little bit more?

Ryan Fetterman: 9:50

So the characterization of the prompt from the first line is telling the, the model that they are acting as a forensic intelligence analyst. And I think this is kind of a creative framing for this kind of task, because they don't want to characterize this task as anything kind of overtly malicious, when they're trying to use a frontier model, which they're trying to use Claude for this on the first pass. So I think this characterization of being an intelligence analyst kind of puts it in a more benign light. They also really emphasize citations, sticking to the facts. Not making any jumps in in inference, they kind of bundle evidence into different layers where there are, subjective identifiers. There are corroborated facts. When you have points of data that are backed by two independent data sources. So this is a pretty thorough structure. Almost like a, you know, a realistic like intelligence assessment type of report that they're putting together. But then, yeah, ultimately, what sticks out about your profile that the LLM is putting together based on the scraped data is who who they are the victim in this case, what they do. What they're worth. Which is a list of your value valuables ranked by monetization, like your crypto. They'll do a lookup on your Roblox account. They'll look at your card accounts, and they'll put these into tears. Low, medium and high. And then they're also assessing your OpSec. How strong are your passwords? Are you using multi-factor authentication? Do you have any privacy tools installed? So it's yeah, pretty comprehensive and a little bit creepy, right?

Amy Ciminnisi: 11:48

And speaking of outsourcing, you mentioned in the blog that you think that this could be a commodity malware. So the owner is selling access to it. People are buying it. So if it is, what might be like the potential reasons that someone wouldn't want to use the integrated LLM. You mentioned it's optional, but that seems like a huge differentiator or value add for someone who's interested in buying it.

Ryan Fetterman: 12:16

Yeah, I mean, as far as I can tell, like the limitations would be just do you have keys for these services? Do you want to tie yourself to, another piece for like attribution or something else that can get you flagged for abuse? So you would need an open router key in this case to use the models. And I guess it depends on the scale of the operation that you're running. Like there would be cost for tokens and things like that. And it's ultimately a question of like what is the actual value add of the AI integration in this case. So I thought initially that this would lead to the attackers being more effective at, successfully stealing from their most high profile targets, because they're going to be able to identify who those targets are faster. But I was thinking about that as from the perspective of like, their tokens and their authentication kind of aging out over time. But if the attacker is able to play the sessions from the victim's own box, it's probably not as big of a deal that those sessions will probably stay active for much longer periods of time. So I think it is, yeah, mostly about running an operation at scale. And maybe not everyone wants to to do something that broad.

Amy Ciminnisi: 13:43

Yeah. And like for practitioners who are listening to this like the fact that VOLTA is self deleting and it doesn't use the usual, command and control traffic is a bit of a headache. So like if you are a defender, where do you even start looking to catch something that's doing all of its sorting kind of in the background?

Ryan Fetterman: 14:05

Yeah. The primary binary will be self deleting the it has a lot of traditional stealer capabilities. So for more mature organizations like there should be detections and things for kind of the well known trade craft here like Alsace dumping or accessing registry, things like that. But this seems like a more targeting like individuals. So in that case, like if you suspect that you've been compromised, there is a file that gets dropped, a VOLTA D debug text file that actually tells you what was collected and will confirm whether you, you had been compromised by this kind of malware. And it also tells you whether the call was successful. It's hard to say what like what's going to be most effective, outside of those other kind of security flags. I think you can try to save the headless mode for Chrome, which I think you can do through, like your registry in windows or on Mac. And I think that would be how the attacker would be accessing like and replaying kind of your browser based like authenticated sessions. So that was kind of the best idea that I had that, that might like get ahead of this.

Amy Ciminnisi: 15:28

Kind of continuing that train of thought. I'm thinking about like, especially because it is so focused on individuals, especially with so many other, things to worry about right now. Do we have any kind of clue on how widespread this specific stealer might be? I don't know, it's so subjective, but do you feel like it's, you know, worth devoting resources to defend against? You know, like how how can the everyday person kind of defend against this? I know I'm asking the hard questions here, but.

Ryan Fetterman: 16:08

Yeah, I think the best approach is to just not click on any links and not open any files and you'll be totally fine. So yeah, you can do what you need to do effectively without clicking on any links on the internet. You'll be safe. I don't think we should overreact. Like, this is, you know, mostly like a mature but commodity stealer that does a lot of things that other, other malware is probably already doing. And it's only like getting this attention because of the disturbing peek behind the curtain into, like, what the developer of this is instructing it to do and kind of this new flavor of AI implementation. But otherwise, like, there's nothing novel here in like the actual attack. So still basic hygiene and safety like online. Don't click on suspicious links. Don't open suspicious attachments. Yeah. Consider like using a sandbox or, sandboxing like internet activity from when your, doing kind of sensitive things like banking or I know people can maintain separate browsers depending on what they're doing.

Amy Ciminnisi: 17:24

Back to the basics.

Ryan Fetterman: 17:26

Y eah.

Amy Ciminnisi: 17:26

As everything is. Looking toward where this might be headed. I mean, do you have any ideas about, you know, potential implications for the future? You know, different ways that this could be leveraged or that this can be developed further.

Ryan Fetterman: 17:46

I mean, it feels like a Black Mirror episode is like where we're headed with these kind of malware findings. I don't want to speculate too much. I mean, I'm trying to stay objective and just see what's happening and only draw conclusions from what we're what we're actually seeing out there. Yeah. Again, I think what was interesting to me was like seeing this in more of a, a cyber crime context, where the AI wasn't adding to the actual capability of the malware per se, but was used in more of that, like human context and offloading the analytical work of the attacker. So I think that will be interesting to keep an eye on if we start to see more things like that. Again, I think the the multi-model architecture was interesting and something that I've seen across multiple samples. Now that these attackers are anticipating hitting model refusals and planning for that and having these kind of cascading implementations where they can relay their request to more permissible models until they get something to work. And that also, I think, tells us that there still are reasons that they want to use these frontier or hosted models versus hosting them them selves, which has been kind of an open question. If open weight models are roughly capable or maybe six months behind frontier level capability, they're quite capable at this point. So why aren't we seeing more attackers using open weight models or hosting their own infrastructure? So I think that that tells us something about their preference for using these open and trusted services without the need to tie or spin up any infrastructure themselves, versus just continue to operate on these platforms like Discord and Telegram and Open Router, where maybe they just get flagged for abuse and get their their keys revoked without any further consequences.

Amy Ciminnisi: 19:48

Right. Oh man, that's fascinating. I feel like that could be an entire other podcast episode in itself. Ryan, thank you so much for joining.

Ryan Fetterman: 19:58

Of course. Anytime. Thank you.

Amy Ciminnisi: 19:59

Listeners. If you'd like to learn more about VOLTA, you can see Ryan's blog at blog.talosintelligence.com. Ryan has also been interviewed by WIRED for a news story that went out on Saturday the 31st, so I will include both of those in the show notes. We'll see you next time. And until then, stay safe out there.

articles.title: Appraisal by AI: Model-driven victim prioritization in the VOLTA infostealer
articles.context: The novelty in the AI-integration is that it is not supporting a traditional malware capability but working as an intelligence analyst on behalf of the operator
articles.full_text:
VOLTA is a mature stealer implant with an optional AI-integration layer. After stealing credentials, sessions, and cryptocurrency wallets, VOLTA sends a structured evidence bundle to an LLM to rank the victim’s assets by monetization value.

If a model refuses to perform the target assessment, VOLTA fails over to a three-model chain, implying a direct engineering effort and expectation of hitting model guardrails.

This stealer is self-deleting, and there is no attacker-owned infrastructure. The novelty in the AI-integration is that it is not supporting a traditional malware capability but working as an intelligence analyst on behalf of the operator.

There is a new idea in the cybercrime world — cast a wide net, steal everything, and let AI sort out the specifics. A new malware self-named “VOLTA-AUTODOXER,” surfaced through the CAIRN research effort, is a self-deleting Windows infostealer that augments its post-theft workflow with an LLM-powered victim-profiling stage.

After harvesting the standard stealer haul, including browser passwords; cookies; payment cards; cryptocurrency wallet seed phrases; Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions; Microsoft OAuth tokens; SSH and cloud-provider keys; Wi-Fi profiles; and screenshots, VOLTA builds a structured evidence bundle about the person behind the machine. This bundle contains geolocation and home address, employer and employer domain, inferred birth year, card last-4 digits, Slack workspaces, document authorship metadata, iPhone backup indicators, and a live Roblox account valuation. It then uses stolen session access to enrich that bundle further: searching the victim's Gmail for purchase receipts to corroborate a home address, pulling UberEats and DoorDash order history, and enriching Discord accounts via the stolen token.

The bundle is serialized and POSTed to OpenRouter under a system prompt that instructs the model to act as "a forensic intelligence analyst drafting a target assessment." The required output includes a section titled “WHAT THEY'RE WORTH” with valuables ranked by monetization with a low/medium/high tier, and a section on “THEIR OPSEC” containing an assessment of the victim's security posture and password hygiene. The model is the operator's triage analyst; it turns a raw credential log into a prioritized and citation-backed dossier of the victim and their monetizable assets.

Figure 1. The VOLTA-AUTODOXER workflow.

The AI configuration: “Go deep, not wide... Be blunt, specific, accurate.”

VOLTA uses a multi-model architecture to fall back resiliently if it hits a model’s refusal, checking each response for phrases like “I can’t” or “I’m not able,” before passing on to a chain of up to three models.

Endpoint

https[:]//openrouter[.]ai/api/v1/chat/completions

Default model

anthropic/claude-opus-4.6

Fallback chain

moonshotai/kimi-k2 → google/gemini-2.5-flash

Temperature

0.2 — deterministic, consistent output

Request format

Hand-assembled JSON; no SDK; User-Agent Mozilla/5.0

Figure 2. Hardcoded model selection.Figure 3. Failover model selection to kimi-k2, and then gemini-2.5-flash.

Model temperate controls the randomness and predictability of LLM-generated text. The low hardcoded temperature value (0.2) suggests the attacker is emphasizing accuracy and consistency. The malware also employs a chain of cascading models in the event of failures. This multi-model architecture suggests that the operator is anticipating encountering refusals, with the fallback pivoting to a few, smaller, and more permissive models.

The system prompt directly reveals the operator’s use case: Produce a concise analytical assessment of the victim’s suitability as a target, backed by an auditable trail of citations.

Figure 4. VOLTA's raw system prompt.

The prompt also asks for something out of the ordinary, but that agents excel at: making connections between sparse and disparate data. For example, encouraging connections like the victim’s names, addresses, or universities to patterns in their passwords. In this case, the model isn't being asked to find data; rather, it’s being asked to stretch the data and make useful inferences that extend the value of what has been scraped.

Stealer capabilities

VOLTA’s capabilities are directly aligned with the records produced in modern digital life, and well beyond basic credential theft. In a single pass, the stealer can extract browser credentials, cookies, and saved payment cards across Chromium-based browsers. It hits Firefox and Thunderbird, Outlook profiles, Slack workspaces, Steam and Battle.net sessions, Discord tokens, Telegram sessions, Roblox accounts, and SSH and cloud-provider config files (gcloud, OpenVPN, Hide.me). VOLTA doesn’t just copy cryptocurrency wallets, but runs an embedded cracker against the vault inline, writing the result to a WALLET VAULTS CRACKED line in its own report.

Every saved Wi-Fi password on the machine is pulled via a direct call to WlanGetProfileList and dumped to plaintext.

Figure 5. VOLTA dumps plaintext passwords for every saved Wi-Fi network on the host.Figure 6. The organized collection targets.

What really sets VOLTA apart from commodity stealers is what comes after the initial collection. There is a live enrichment pass that leverages stolen sessions to deep dive the victim’s data. For example, using the victim's own authenticated Gmail tokens, it queries their inbox for receipts from Amazon, DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, Walmart, and PayPal, then review those receipts to establish a confirmed home address. Stolen Uber Eats and DoorDash sessions are called directly for order history. The Discord token is re-used to enrich the victim's account profile. Roblox inventory is valued via a live “Rolimons[.]com” lookup.

Figure 7. That’s right: Your Uber Eats history is now a potential liability.

After the collection and enrichment stages are complete, the data is assembled and structured locally in a file called “Identity_Report.txt”. This file is serialized into a bundle as JSON and POSTed to OpenRouter along with the system prompt. The returned payload is received as “AI_Analysis.txt”. Both files exfil together in “volta_dox.zip”.

Figure 8. VOLTA’s exfil can happen in three stages: 1) after the stealer runs (“volta_log.zip”), 2) after the AI call (“volta_dox.zip”), (3) if the network enrichment produces anything (“volta_doxnet.zip”).

The inference round-trip happens entirely through the victim's own network connection, on their own machine, before the result is exfiltrated.

Deployment model

Instead of hardcoding its Telegram channel, API keys, and settings directly into the code (which is likely what someone writing a tool for personal use would do) VOLTA uses a template with six swappable slots, filled in at build time.

This suggests it’s a builder model: The author sells access, the customer provides their values, and the builder compiles a custom binary for each order. The credentials in those slots are encrypted, but not in a meaningful way. The key is SHA-256 of two constants sitting in the same binary, but it's presumably there because customers expect their API keys not to be sitting in plaintext, not because it provides real protection. Anyone who reverses the file can recover them.

If VOLTA is indeed a commoditized malware, then the AI dossier capability isn't something the author invented for their own operations. It is a feature which enables a customer of any level of sophistication to point it at victims and start receiving ranked target assessments in their Telegram inbox.

All the observed endpoints for this malware are third-party controlled. There is no actor-owned infrastructure.

Countermeasures

Much of the token-stealing capability of VOLTA relies on techniques to bypass App-Bound Encryption (ABE) in Chrome. An application control policy that restricts which processes may launch Chrome with --headless would block the ABE decryption path entirely. At minimum, you can also alert when Chrome is launched with --headless from any process not in a known developer. Best practices for storing credentials in hardware backed stores also apply.

In the event of compromise, the main executable may have deleted itself, but users should attempt to preserve the “APPDATA%\volta_debug.txt” file. This is a timestamped harvest log and contains a record of exactly what was collected and whether the LLM call succeeded. Revoke any potentially compromised tokens and change passwords. For cryptocurrency wallets, if the seed phrase was in plaintext on disk, treat the wallet as fully compromised and migrate funds to a new wallet with a seed generated on an air-gapped device.

Conclusions

VOLTA is a mature stealer with a late-stage AI layer added for one purpose: relieving the operator of analytical work. The axis of AI improvement here is not speed or scale but effort displacement; the same logic visible in CLOSEDQUORUM, though applied to a different phase. These implants reflect the same underlying logic: Identify the step that requires the most sustained human attention and replace it with a model call. The question for defenders is not whether this pattern will appear elsewhere, but which phase it touches next.

Figure 9. End-to-end VOLTA workflow.

The second trend to watch is the anticipation of hitting model refusals, and the approaches to building in resiliency. In this case, it includes a fallback chain from Claude to Kimi to Gemini and the ability to run without the LLM stage altogether if no key is present. As AI integration in malware matures, refusal resilience may become a standard design requirement.

The open question underlying both trends is whether effort displacement in crimeware changes the landscape in a meaningful way: lowering the operational floor, raising the ceiling on scale, or both. Cybercrime operations have always been opportunistic, and the sophistication bar has always been lower than assumed, but there is a difference between a wide net and a wide net that sorts itself.

Welcome to this week’s edition of the Threat Source newsletter.

“The darkest period of my life, so far, arrived the summer I was pregnant with my eldest son. The future was growing in me with all of its terrifying unpredictability, and I found myself anxious, unable to work and woefully at sea.” — Lauren Groff

I doubt Lauren had this maniacal infosec news cycle in mind when she wrote about the terrifyingly unpredictable future, but honestly, she’s got our current careers down cold. Let he who is not woefully at sea cast the first water balloon? I’ll work on it. Here we are with PHP taking up every available ounce of oxygen, Node.js adding its own spice to the sauce... and here’s me, staring my screen blankly, waiting for an original thought to leak out and onto this page. Not to worry, none have. There is simply nothing novel to say because the entire internet has it covered. In triplicate. With graphs and compelling statistics and AI-generated evil bad guy images galore.

These vulnerabilities are serious, and the remediations matter. Teams need to know what they run, find the affected systems, and get them patched and determine ways to secure systems that can’t be patched. I’m simply not going to add another dramatic headline to the stack or pretend there’s a clever new angle hiding in the margins. The thing I keep looping on is that the work underneath the headlines is familiar and it’s the real story. To defend your environment, you need a team that knows that environment, has enough time and expertise to investigate the telemetry, that can tell an anomaly from the usual benign noise, and take action. Yes, the right tools help, and without them you can’t do it — but the people doing the work are still what make those tools useful.

Give smart people enough room to do smart people stuff. This is the entire ballgame. Read it again: Give smart people enough room to do smart people stuff. Because a good response starts way before the headline. Know what you own, who owns it, what version is running, whether it can be reached from the internet, what identities can do what task on the device, etc. When a fix is available, make sure it actually reaches the system you meant to fix. If a system cannot be updated yet, give that exception an owner and a deadline. Reduce its exposure, add monitoring, and keep checking until the fix is in place. “We’ll get to it” is not a plan.

So, there may be nothing new to say about PHP this week, but the work is still worth talking about: Know your environment, take care of your team members, and keep paying attention when the weird thing stops being weird and starts becoming evidence. When the next headline arrives, help your teammate do the same.

“The only thing that makes life possible is permanent, intolerable uncertainty: not knowing what comes next.” — Ursula K. Le Guin

The one big thing

Cisco Talos has recently discovered "NIK C2," a new command-and-control framework that integrates AI directly into its attack chain. This Go-based Windows implant allows adversaries to dump credentials, stream keystrokes, and deploy screen-locking ransomware. It also uses an integrated OpenAI model to analyze harvested data on the fly. By hijacking the victim's own API keys to fund these requests, NIK C2 collapses data collection and exploitation into a single, continuous session.

Why do I care?

By embedding a live AI pipeline directly into the C2 loop, NIK C2 turns a compromised host into an active operational asset rather than a passive foothold. Because it processes data and generates context-aware payloads locally, it erases the offline processing delays that historically gave defenders a critical detection window. Furthermore, by piggybacking on the victim's OpenAI account, threat actors completely mask their infrastructure, leaving no attributable trace and complicating incident response.

So now what?

Defenders must embrace continuous behavioral vigilance. Ensure endpoint solutions monitor for unusual local proxy routing, unexpected PowerShell executions, and unauthorized access to browser databases or crypto wallets. Update your defenses using the ClamAV signature and indicators of compromise (IOCs) provided in the full blog.

Top security headlines of the week

CISA gives agencies days to patch critical PHP bugs CISA added the two vulnerabilities in the PHP open-source scripting software to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog Monday. (Federal News Network)

Node2Shell: Brotli flaw triggers patching across Microsoft, Node.js, Python packagesAn out-of-bounds write in Google’s Brotli decoder affects Node.js, .NET, PowerShell, and Python packages, and can lead to code execution. (SecurityWeek)

Gheist uses stolen GitHub tokens to steal private repository secrets via Actions logs Each workflow sits on a new branch named ci-sync- followed by six random characters. Deleting a branch, or the run it started, does not undo the exposure. (The Hacker News)

Japan internet giant GMO says hackers posted stolen customer data GMO Internet is investigating a data leak after suspected unauthorized access to its Onamae cloud desktop service, which provides virtualized desktops to financial traders. (TechCrunch)

Third Serengeti sweep tops 1,400 arrests as investigations mature Interpol's annual Operation Serengeti, now on its third iteration, led to 1,462 arrests across 20 African countries and the U.S., recovering $105 million in stolen funds. (Dark Reading)

Can’t get enough Talos?

Stealing AI secrets and breaking EDRs Phishing may have dropped from last quarter's highs, but ransomware engagements climbed as attackers shifted their focus toward disabling EDR systems and scraping AI credentials. The financial sector also returned as a top target.

From federal SOCs to Talos: Ryan Fetterman on practical security research What does it mean to be "blue collar" for the blue team? Amy sat down with security researcher Ryan Fetterman to discuss his journey from federal agency work to his new role at Talos.

David joins the Beers with Talos crew for a conversation how AI changes about his famous model, how EvidenceForge creates simulated incidents for research and training, and why his red-team entrance exam didn’t go to plan.

articles.title: IR trends Q3 2026: Actors impersonate IT help desks in vishing attacks as ransomware activity increases
articles.context: Threat actors predominantly chose to disable endpoint detection and response (EDR) systems, often by exploiting vulnerable drivers or using Windows Defender Application Control...
articles.full_text:
Phishing remained the leading initial access technique, appearing in slightly over one-third of all Cisco Talos Incident Response (Talos IR) engagements — a decrease from over 50 percent last quarter. In addition to traditional phishing links and attachments, we observed numerous threat actors conducting voice phishing (vishing) in tandem with IT desk impersonation to socially engineer the victim into allowing remote access via a legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool. Exploitation of public-facing applications was the next most common vector, accounting for one-third of Talos IR engagements. Threat actors predominantly targeted edge devices such as security gateways and remote network management interfaces. These are critical components within enterprise environments, often responsible for managing authentication, network traffic, or sensitive data. Compromising them can provide broad access to internal networks or user credentials.

Ransomware and pre-ransomware incidents made up 27 percent of engagements in Q3 2026, an increase from a maximum of 20 percent seen in the previous four quarters. Talos responded to attacks involving prolific, technologically advanced, and well-established ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) variants such as The Gentlemen, Qilin, and Rhysida, as well as Interlock, which operates as a closed group. Threat actors predominantly chose to disable endpoint detection and response (EDR) systems, often by exploiting vulnerable drivers or using Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC). Additionally, we observed the emerging ransomware variant VYPR, whose operator(s) tested a range of tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) instead of following a standard attack method or affiliate playbook.

Salt Typhoon-affiliated threat actors exploit public-facing application vulnerabilities for cyber espionage

Talos IR continues to see prolonged cyber espionage intrusions targeting the telecommunications sector. Talos attributed most of these intrusions with high confidence to China state-sponsored threat actors, including Salt Typhoon. The attackers in these intrusions routinely gain initial access by leveraging valid credentials and exploiting a known vulnerability (CVE-2023-20198) in publicly accessible web-based management interfaces—two of the most frequently observed initial access vectors this quarter. In one campaign, the threat actor deployed BadCandy, a malicious web shell implant known to be leveraged by Salt Typhoon, to maintain persistent and stealthy remote access.

The adversaries continue to employ living-off-the-land (LOTL) tactics, leveraging legitimate network infrastructure features — such as VPN access, traffic mirroring, and management protocols — to establish backdoors, exfiltrate data, and conduct reconnaissance. Exploiting a vulnerability in the web-based management interface, they created privileged accounts, disabled logging to conceal their activity, and altered configurations to maintain persistence, blending their actions with normal administrative operations to evade detection.

These intrusions revealed several security weaknesses in the victim environment, including reliance on password-only authentication without evidence of multi-factor authentication (MFA), use of legacy and weak management protocols (such as plaintext SNMP and outdated VPN encryption), and inadequate credential management practices. Attackers were able to create and abuse privileged accounts, disable logging, and manipulate configuration settings without encountering effective security barriers, enabling persistent and stealthy access. The absence of strong MFA and robust credential management are two of the most frequently observed security weaknesses this quarter.

AI exploited as a weapon and a target

Recent Talos IR investigations highlight the growing role of artificial intelligence (AI) in cybercriminal activity, both as a tool and a target. In one case, an internal threat actor who was hired under false credentials abused their privileged access to install AI-powered development tools, such as GitHub Copilot CLI and Anthropic Claude Code. While the investigation did not find evidence of malicious activity or data theft, the employee’s developer-level access — including cloning repositories, configuring plugins, and connecting to databases — could have enabled them to use AI tools to automate malicious actions within the organization.

A second investigation revealed an attack chain in which a compromised macOS endpoint, infected via a trojanized application, was scripted to scrape credentials from the macOS keychain specifically associated with the Anthropic Claude Code AI assistant. This direct targeting of AI-related secrets highlights an emerging threat, where attackers seek to compromise not only traditional user and system credentials but also those tied to AI platforms, which may grant access to additional sensitive data and advanced automation capabilities.

These incidents highlight the critical need for organizations to implement strong MFA and robust credential management practices, especially for AI platforms and development tools.

Ransomware trends

Ransomware and pre-ransomware incidents increased from a little over 20 percent last quarter to 27 percent in Q3, involving well-known threat groups like Interlock and the emerging ransomware VYPR. Frequently observed techniques involved deleting EDR systems and socially engineering victims into initiating remote management sessions.

Emerging ransomware variant: VYPR

During a Talos IR engagement, we observed a ransomware variant called “VYPR” that we assess is relatively new and still operationally immature. This assessment is supported by the absence of an established data leak site (DLS), as none was referenced in the ransom note and associated DLS infrastructure was not created until after the engagement. The group also appeared to rely on older leaked Conti-derived source code with only minimal modifications, reflecting a relatively unsophisticated technical approach. Their operations further suggested experimentation rather than a refined playbook, as they took an unusually long time to exfiltrate and encrypt data while testing different exfiltration parameters and deploying multiple vulnerable drivers to disable EDR protections.

The actor gained initial access through voice phishing (vishing); they tricked a user into initiating a Microsoft Quick Assist session, allowing remote access to the endpoint. While the exact social engineering technique was not confirmed in this case, threat actors frequently impersonate IT help desks during vishing calls to manipulate victims into establishing remote connections — a tactic observed in several other Q3 engagements.

The actor was then able to utilize existing RMM software, which subsequently executed PowerShell commands to download and install a Microsoft Software Installer (MSI) package from a remote IP address. During the attack, the actor leveraged tools that are commonly observed during ransomware investigations, including MeshAgent, Rclone, PsExec, IP scan, and Microsoft Terminal Services Client (MSTSC). Notably, we saw exfiltration over multiple days, which is not commonly observed during ransomware investigations.

EDR killers: Why evade detection when you can destroy it?

We observed several instances where ransomware operators disabled EDR systems, prioritizing direct disruption of security controls. We observed Interlock ransomware actors making multiple attempts to impair endpoint detection EDR capabilities by trying to uninstall Cisco Secure Endpoint (CSE) on compromised systems and used tools such as PsExec.exe and taskkill.exe to terminate security services and integrity checkers, including cscm.exe and sfc.exe. Additionally, the adversary disabled Windows Defender real-time protection and cleared various event logs to reduce visibility and hinder forensic analysis. This is in line with previously observed Interlock activity, where they deployed a malicious WDAC policy to terminate EDR solutions.

In the previously mentioned VYPR ransomware incident, the threat actor disabled EDR and antivirus (AV) by using Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD) techniques to evade detection and execute the ransomware. BYOVD attacks take advantage of trusted but flawed drivers to gain kernel-level access, enabling threat actors to disable EDR mechanisms and carry out their operations unimpeded. While this technique is commonly observed in ransomware attacks, this actor deployed an unusually large number of vulnerable drivers in the environment, possibly to create redundancies and maximize their chances of success.

Targeting

Targeting of the financial industry increased from last quarter to comprise 18 percent of all engagements, tying with public administration as the most targeted sector. Although the financial industry remains a valuable target, Talos has not ranked it among the top three most impacted sectors since 2024. One possible reason is that organizations in finance can typically invest more in cybersecurity, unlike sectors such as public administration, which has consistently been among the top-targeted industries over the past year. Meanwhile, health care fell to third place after ranking as the most targeted industry for the previous two consecutive quarters.

Initial access

While the number of engagements involving phishing as an initial access vector declined from last quarter, it remained the most common technique, appearing in 37 percent of Talos IR engagements. Exploitation of public-facing applications was the second most common initial access vector, accounting for 33 percent of engagements.

Recommendations for addressing top security weaknesses

The most common security weaknesses observed this quarter were insufficient logging, improper credential and secret management, and absent or improperly implemented authentication and MFA. These trends closely mirror last quarter, when insufficient logging and authentication weaknesses were also prevalent.

Centralize logging and set retention requirements

The leading security weakness was insufficient logging leading to visibility gaps, seen in over 40 percent of engagements this quarter. These gaps were in part due to the common threat actor practice of deleting logs, and in part due to insufficient log retention or configuration implemented by the customer. Talos IR recommends implementing a SIEM or centralized logging platform with a minimum of 90 days of retention, forwarding logs from servers, workstations, network infrastructure, cloud identity providers, and security appliances off-device so they survive log tampering and host rebuilds, and enabling process-creation, command-line, and cloud API (e.g., Microsoft Graph) auditing. Talos IR's Log Architecture Assessment service can identify gaps and provide a roadmap to a complete view of the environment.

Tighten authentication and MFA controls

Missing or insufficient authentication and MFA controls were the third most common security weakness this quarter, observed in 33 percent of engagements. The most prevalent issue was reliance on single-factor authentication, which allowed unauthorized access in several incidents. In many cases, legacy authentication protocols were still enabled, enabling adversaries to log in without any MFA requirements, and some environments failed to enforce MFA for high-privilege accounts. To reduce this risk, Talos IR recommends transitioning from push- and SMS-based MFA to phishing-resistant methods such as FIDO2/WebAuthn and hardware security keys. Organizations should also restrict self-service MFA enrollment by requiring helpdesk verification, block legacy authentication through Conditional Access, enforce number matching or verified push where phishing-resistant methods are not yet feasible, and condition access on device compliance and trusted infrastructure rather than geographic location alone.

Safeguard credentials and secrets

Improper credential and secret management was the second most common security weakness seen in 33 percent of engagements this quarter, reinforcing the importance of security awareness training and consistent security hygiene for every user. Observed security issues included unsafe storage and handling of credentials, such as saving passwords in browser stores, poor control mechanisms like permitting autofill for browser-stored credentials, and credential reuse and sharing. Effective secret management begins with a formal process that covers passwords, API keys, tokens, certificates, and other sensitive credentials. By requiring unique passwords for every account and encouraging the use of password managers, organizations reduce the risks associated with credential reuse and sharing. Storing secrets securely, with encryption and access restricted to only those who need them, further strengthens protection. When credentials are no longer necessary or are suspected to be compromised, they should be promptly revoked and replaced. Regular reviews of access to privileged credentials, combined with thorough logging, help detect unusual activity. Equipping staff with training on safe handling and clear reporting procedures ensures that accidental disclosures are addressed quickly and effectively.

Tales from the Frontlines: An exclusive briefing on Q3 incidents

On November 12, Talos incident responders will be hosting an exclusive, unrecorded 30-minute webinar to review the most high-impact incidents our customers faced in Q3. Designed for security professionals of all levels, this is a candid discussion of what happened, how we handled it, and what it means for your organization.

Registration is required to attend. Don't miss this chance to hear real-world stories from the frontlines of cyber defense, directly from the team who lived them.

Register here

MITRE ATT&CK appendix

The table below represents MITRE ATT&CK techniques and tools observed in this quarter’s IR engagements, including relevant examples. Given that some techniques can fall under multiple tactics, we grouped them under the most relevant tactic based on the way they were leveraged. Please note that this is not an exhaustive list.

Key findings from the MITRE ATT&CK framework include:

The rise of phishing and the frequent use of valid accounts for initial access and lateral movement both highlight how attackers continue to rely on methods that have remained consistently effective year over year.

Attacker success consistently reflects basic weaknesses in enterprise security posture, with persistent exploitation of known vulnerabilities — especially in internet-facing applications — demonstrating that adversaries continually scan for and opportunistically target unpatched systems.

The most used techniques to maintain persistence were deploying web shells and creating scheduled tasks, demonstrating that attackers prioritize stealthy, reliable access by leveraging legitimate system components that blend in with normal operations. These techniques enable threat actors to maintain long-term control and quickly re-establish their presence even if some signs of compromise are removed.

articles.full_text:
Cisco Talos observed a new AI-integrated command-and-control (C2) framework in the wild called “NIK C2.”

NIK C2 contains a Windows implant, using which, an actor can dump credentials, stream the victim's keystrokes to collect the targeted victim’s sensitive data, and instruct an integrated AI model to analyze the harvested data, all within the compromised session.

In this framework, the actor has abused the OpenAI Chat Completions application programming interface (API), which is a HTTP endpoint that enables ChatGPT-style conversations programmatically.

In addition to the features that enable theft, an actor can also deploy desktop screen-locking ransomware via the NIK C2 implant onto the victim machine, leading to a ransom demand in Bitcoin or USDT cryptocurrencies.

NIK C2 reshapes adversary tradecraft by collapsing collection and exploitation into a single continuous session, effectively erasing the offline processing delays that historically granted defenders critical detection windows.

Such AI-enabled adversarial frameworks require defenders to move beyond traditional detection and embrace continuous behavioral vigilance as the new baseline.

NIK C2 implant: AI-integrated remote access tool

The NIK C2 implant is a Go-based, 64-bit Windows remote access tool that grants persistent control over compromised hosts using a resilient dual-channel C2 architecture. It communicates over TLS-secured WebSockets on port 443 alongside an HTTP fallback polling loop every 250 milliseconds, protecting all traffic with AES-256-GCM encryption derived from a hardcoded seed. To survive takedowns, the implant routes traffic across three prioritized C2 tiers, which are runtime-updated URLs, an embedded encrypted server list, and a hardcoded fallback address. Beyond standard operations, the implant features surveillance, theft, lateral movement, and evasion capabilities, including credential dumping, RDP session hijacking, process hollowing, and a C2-driven screen lock ransomware module.

Notably, the NIK C2 implant embeds a fully integrated OpenAI API client via its ai_generate command, allowing operators to route arbitrary prompts to the OpenAI Chat Completions API directly through the infected host. The NIK C2 implant manages API key resolution, request assembly, and response parsing locally, returning the encrypted generative AI results to the actor's C2.

The observed NIK C2 implant samples in the wild contains an embedded build path (/opt/nik_panel/data/build_52b79724a1fc4b8f/main.go), which identifies the project as "nik_panel" and indicates that the implant was cross compiled for Windows from a Linux development environment. Furthermore, the embedded eight-byte hex token matching the build identifier highlights that the threat actor's infrastructure actively tracking and versioning the implants.

Figure 1. NIK C2 implant’s operational architecture.

NIK C2 implant evolution timeline

Talos observed that the NIK C2 implant development trajectory spans at least three distinct versions. All binaries observed in the wild were compiled with Go 1.23.4 (which was released in December 2024), placing the entire sample set compiled no earlier than late 2024. The actor has Zeroed PE TimeDateStamp fields and near-epoch filesystem timestamps (manifesting as Nov 29, 1979) are applied consistently across all samples.

We developed a timeline based on the initial sighting dates of NIK C2 implant variants in OSINT.

Figure 2. NIK C2 implant evolution timeline.

The pace of capability addition across the three versions indicates a technically proficient team with prior malware operations experience is actively expanding NIK C2 towards a full-service adversarial framework.

Active NIK C2 server seen in the wild

During our research, we observed that a threat actor hosted the NIK C2 framework on a server at IP address “87.120.196[.]120”, resolving the domain “total-sitevv[.]lol”. The C2 server hosted an SSL/TLS certificate (serial number 7d16381a9de823943b5a0987dbd0f26edf22052b and jarm:"28d28d28d00000000042d42d0000001f361a1bf80ed39a1e352adeb016a07b" ) with the Common Name (CN) set to nik-panel. This CN value matches strings embedded within the implant binary. Observing the NIK C2 infrastructure active in the wild allowed us to assess with moderate confidence that NIK C2 is not merely a proof of concept, but a fully functional, AI-integrated C2 framework.

Figure 3. NIK C2 was observed in the wild during the research period.

NIK C2 implant integrates OpenAI’s API

AI integration is one of the most architecturally distinct features of NIK C2 implant. It constructs a fully formed HTTP request to OpenAI’s production inference endpoint, transmits it from the victim machine IP address, parses the JSON response, and returns the AI-generated text to the actor’s panel. The entire operation from receiving the actor prompt to returning the large language model (LLM) reply is executed synchronously with a 60-second timeout.

The implant begins by extracting three fields from the command payload received from the C2. The first field, identified by the key prompt, is the text the actor wants to send to the AI model. If the prompt string has zero length, the handler immediately constructs an error response and returns without making any outbound network call. The second field, identified by the key api_key is the OpenAI API key to use for authentication. The third field, identified by the key model, specifies which OpenAI model to use.

Figure 4. Snippet of NIK C2 implant AI handler module.

After extracting the three parameters, the implant checks whether the actor supplied an API key. If not, it calls the operating system's environment variable reader with the string OPENAI_API_KEY and uses the victim’s API key. This fallback is not a backup mechanism for API key resolution. It is a deliberate design with significant operational implications. If the victim has configured an OpenAI account on their machine, that account's API key will be used to fund the actor's AI inference. OpenAI's billing system will charge the victim's payment method, and OpenAI's access logs will show the victim's API key as the one that made the requests, allowing no trace attributable to the threat actor.

If the actor does not specify a model name, the implant falls back to a five-character default string stored in the binary data section. Decoding the five-character value showed gpt-4 confirming that GPT4 is the default when no model is specified. The actor can override this by passing any valid OpenAI model identifier in the command payload, allowing selection of newer models as they become available without requiring a binary update.

The implant builds the OpenAI API request body by constructing a map with four fields. The first field uses the key model and contains the resolved model name. The second field uses key messages and contains a two-element array of message maps. The third field uses the key temperature and contains a floating-point value read from a constant in the binary data section. The fourth field uses the key max_tokens and contains an integer value also read from binary.

The message array is constructed in the order that the OpenAI Chat Completions API expects. The system message is first followed by the user message. The system message map has the role system and a content string that is exactly 68 bytes long hardcoded in the binary. This 68-byte string is the implant's behavioral instruction to the AI. It defines the model's operational role and response style for the duration of the session. The user message map has the role user and contains the actor's prompt text verbiage. The complete map structure is then serialized to JSON. The JSON message is sent to the URL https:// api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions, the OpenAI Chat Completions endpoint, through an HTTP POST request.

Figure 5. Snippet of NIK C2 implant AI handler module.

When the HTTP response arrives with a 200 status code, the handler uses Golang's JSON decoder to parse the response body directly into a generic map structure without defining a typed schema. It then navigates the decoded map by string key lookups in the sequence that the OpenAI Chat Completions API response structure defines. The outermost map is queried for the key choices which in a successful response contains an array. The implant checks that this array is non-empty, then accesses its element keys message and content. The string value at key content is the AI model-generated text response.

After successfully extracting the AI-generated content, the handler assembles a result map with four entries. The key status is set to a constant string that reads as generated. The key code is set to the AI model's response text, so that the actor receives the full content of the model’s replies. The key model is set to the resolved model name that was used for the request, confirming which model produced the output. The key usage is set to the raw usage object from the OpenAI response, which contains the prompt token count, completion token count, and total token count. This usage data allows the actor to track how many tokens are consumed per request. The completed result map is ultimately transmitted to the C2 server over WebSocket or through the HTTP fallback C2 address.

Figure 6. AI model response is encapsulated in JSON message and will be sent to C2.

Dual execution modes of NIK C2 implant

Upon execution, the implant inspects its command-line arguments to determine its execution path. The argument watchdog activates supervisory monitoring to relaunch the core process if terminated, the copywatchdog tracks file copy operations, and the absence of either defaults execution to primary agent mode.

In primary mode, it uses a named mutex to enforce single-instance execution, logs a message reading [NIK] Starting, generates a 32-byte cryptographic session key if uninitialized, decodes its obfuscated C2 address, and sets its masquerade name to “svchost.exe” or “simvol.exe”.

After initial setup, the binary records its process ID (PID) in the victim's temporary application folder and executes its persistence and evasion routines. These routines include copying to %appdata%/Roaming/Microsoft/Network with modified access controls, configuring Windows autostart registry entries, and masquerading its process. Finally, it starts the local proxy server, initiates the WebSocket communication loop in a separate goroutine, and enters a continuous heartbeat polling loop on the main thread.

Implant’s C2 command surface overview

The implant command dispatcher module facilitates over 52 commands that are directed by the C2 panel. The dispatcher module uses byte-level string matching to map the associated modules that are launched as concurrent goroutines, allowing multiple operations to run in parallel.

Implant deploys screen-locking ransomware

The ransomware module of the implant operates as a multi-stage attack controller that the actor runs in sequence to prepare, deploy, and retract a screen-locking ransomware payload.

At first, it executes PowerShell to execute a raw disk copy command that reads directly from the physical drive device path (“\\.\PhysicalDrive0”) and writes the first sector, which is Master Boot Record (MBR), to a file named “mbr_backup.bin” in the Windows temporary directory.

Figure 7. Snippet of NIK C2 implant’s boot ransomware handler function.

Next, the module constructs a complete self-contained HTML lock screen code entirely at runtime from a hardcoded format string, parameterized with actor supplied Bitcoin and USDT wallet addresses, prices, contact email, timer duration, and custom text from the C2 command message, allowing the actor to fully customize the ransom demands.

Figure 8. Screenlocker HTML code is hardcoded in NIK C2 implant binary.

After generating the HTML code, the binary writes it to the file “lock_screen.html” in the system temporary directory. It then generates a Windows batch script that calls mshta.exe with the path to the HTML file, followed by an infinite loop construct with a five-second timeout between iterations, ensuring that if the user somehow closes the window it reopens within five seconds. This batch file is written to the temp directory as “lock_start.bat”.

The implant then runs a reg add command that writes a registry Run key named “SystemLock” under the current user's autostart path, pointing to a cmd /c invocation of the batch file, so the lock screen is executed on every user's logon. Additionally, a background goroutine is spawned that continuously monitors and relaunches the lock screen process. Finally, the module sends a confirmation response to C2 with the path of the deployed HTML file and the timer value.

The design of this ransomware module is notable for several reasons. It does not encrypt any files, which means it leaves no forensic trail of file modification timestamps or encryption markers. It relies entirely on a screen lock, which is considerably faster to deploy than a file encryption ransomware. The persistence via registry Run key and a self-healing loop ensures the screen lock survives user attempts to dismiss it and survives a system restart.

Figure 9. Desktop lockscreen page of the ransomware deployed by the NIK C2 implant.

Implant’s bootkit preparation feature

The bootkit preparation module of the implant is designed to survey the victim machine's boot firmware environment and then stage a bootkit payload file.

It executes bcdedit /enum, the Windows Boot Configuration Data editor, with the output flag that enumerates all boot entries while hiding the console window. The implant reads the full output and searches for three specific substrings in sequence including EFI, Windows Boot Manager, and Windows Legacy OS Loader. If any of these are found, the boot type is classified as UEFI. The binary also searches for ntldr, the legacy Windows NT loader used by BIOS-mode systems as a fallback. Based on which string was matched, the boot type is recorded as either "UEFI" or "BIOS" as a string of the appropriate length. Separately, the binary runs a PowerShell command invoking Confirm-SecureBootUEFI, which is a built-in PowerShell command that returns to the current Secure Boot state. The output is searched for the string True to detect an enabled Secure Boot and for False to detect an explicitly disabled Secure Boot. If neither is present, the value is recorded as unknown. The result is sent back to the C2, a map containing the boot type classification and the Secure Boot status string.

Then the implant writes a 16-byte placeholder file named “bootkit.bin” to the system temporary directory. The bytes written spell out "NIK_BOOTKIT_PREP" in ASCII, which serves as a staging marker rather than an actual bootkit binary. This placeholder confirms that the target path is writable by the current process, establishes the file location that subsequent operations will reference, and can be overwritten by the actual bootkit binary delivered through the implant's file-upload or file-write command handlers. The path to the staged file is returned to the C2 in response.

Implant’s theft functionality

When the actor issues the theft category commands from the C2, the implant executes the associated goroutines to collect the targeted data into a result map space in the victim machine memory:

WiFi password theft (wifi_steal)

The implant executes netsh commands directly via Go’s exec.Command function by passing arguments as discrete tokens rather than through a shell string. Harvested results are formatted under specific labels: plaintext Wi-Fi passwords appear under Key Content:, saved network names are cataloged under WiFi Profiles: (with missing entries flagged using the per-entry format [%s] not found), and execution failures or absent interfaces return standardized error strings such as [WiFi] no wireless adapter or access denied and No WiFi profiles found.

netsh wlan show profiles netsh wlan show profile name="" key=clear

Browser credential extraction (passwords, quick_steal)

The implant stages targeted browser database files into an archive alongside the Local State file, which contains the AES master key protected by Data Protection Application Programming Interface (DPAPI). The implant imports and executes the CryptUnprotectData Windows API to unwrap the AES key and decrypt the databases locally. Otherwise, it exfiltrates the raw encrypted databases to the C2 server for offline extraction.

The implant extracts Discord tokens and session cookies from the levelDB store on the victim machine. The extracted outputs are labelled as === Discord Tokens === and DISCORD TOKENS. The browser session cookies (Discord_Cookies) are extracted from the copied Cookies database.

Victim’s desktop-based wallets are collected directly from the wallet storage paths. Browser extension wallets are extracted from chromium LevelDB stored by extension ID.

Seed phrase, private key file, and system reconnaissance

The implant performs two regular expression patterns to search on the entire filesystem of the victim machine. These two regular expressions are designed to scan file names for sensitive cryptographic assets and credentials, functioning as case-insensitive patterns ?i. The first expression targets cryptocurrency recovery materials and wallet backups by matching keywords like "seed," "mnemonic," or "wallet" paired with common plain-text and data file extensions (.txt, .md, .csv, .dat), while the second seeks out asymmetric private keys and general secrets using terms like "private," "privkey," or "secret" paired with both text files and standard cryptographic key containers (.key, .pem). Because both patterns use unanchored, greedy matching (.*) without start (^) or end ($) boundary anchors, they capture any file where these sensitive terms precede the target extensions. Matched data are collected under the label of seed candidates and archived into “browserdata.zip”.

(?i)(seed|phrase|mnemonic|recovery|backup|wallet).*(\.txt|\.md|\.csv|\.dat) (?i)(private|privkey|secret).*(\.txt|\.md|\.key|\.pem)
