After all collection paths are complete, the implant assembles all collected data into a single document that looks like a formatted report with clearly labeled sections for each data category such as === CRYPTO ===, === WIFI ===, === BROWSER ===.

Keylogger: Keystrokes livestreamed to C2

The keylogger module of the implant uses a persistent background goroutine that polls all 256 Windows virtual key codes, detecting keypresses via dynamically resolved API calls, and transmits the captured input. When a compromised victim presses a valid key on the keyboard, it is simultaneously streamed live as an AES-256-GCM encrypted JSON payload over WebSocket to C2 and also appends to an in-memory buffer capped at 10,000 entries and halved when full to prevent memory leaks. On an actor's dump command, this buffer is concatenated into a single string and returned to C2 via WebSocket or HTTP fallback, ensuring complete data transfer even during network interruptions.

Stolen data exfiltration to C2

Once the archive is assembled, the entire result map is handed to the result transmission routine of the implant. That routine constructs a new JSON object containing five specific fields. It includes the command identifier echoed back from the original command. It also contains the agent's persistent identifier, formatted as ag_<16 hex chars>. The type field is set to the string quick_steal_response. Finally, the data field holds the complete result map.

Once constructed, this object is forwarded to the encryption routine. The routine serializes the object into JSON. It then generates 12 fresh random bytes to serve as a nonce. Next, it encrypts the serialized JSON using AES-256-GCM with a static key derived from a hardcoded seed. It concatenates the nonce, the ciphertext, and the 16-byte authentication tag and Base64-encodes the entire payload. The encrypted payload is placed in a wrapper object under the "e" key alongside the plain-text agent ID, and the wrapper is JSON marshaled into the final payload.

This encrypted payload is then delivered through an available transmission path. The sending routine first checks whether the WebSocket connection is live. If it is, the payload is written directly into a WebSocket text frame on the existing connection, reaching the actor's panel with minimal latency. If the WebSocket is not currently connected, the routine falls back to an HTTP POST request to the endpoint path /api/c2/result on the C2 server, using the same encrypted body format. This dual-path design ensures stolen data is delivered even during WebSocket interruptions, as the HTTP channel remains functional independently of the WebSocket state.

Implant’s C2 protocol

The implant C2 architecture is designed for two independent, simultaneously operating communication channels. The primary channel is a persistent WebSocket connection over TLS. The secondary channel is an HTTP polling loop that posts to a fixed API endpoint at regular intervals.

With the primary channel, the connection begins with a TCP dial to the C2 server address with an eight-second timeout. If the port is not explicitly present in the configured address, port 443 is appended automatically. Once the TCP socket is established, it is wrapped in a TLS session using a custom certificate configuration that pins to a specific certificate rather than validating against the system's certificate authority store. This prevents standard TLS interception proxies from observing traffic.

Immediately after a successful WebSocket handshake but before any command is received, the implant transmits a full system registration message. The implant collects victim data such as the machine hostname, the local LAN IP address, the Windows username from the environment, a user security identifier, the local reverse-proxy port number that was assigned when the embedded proxy server was started, and the detected upstream proxy configuration derived from the Windows registry proxy settings. All of this is assembled into a JSON object and encrypted and sent to the C2.

Figure 10. Snippet of NIK C2 IMPLANT’s C2 communication handler function.

The HTTP polling channel runs independently. Every approximately 250 milliseconds, the agent collects a fresh snapshot of victim state hostname, watchdog status, local IP, username, current timestamp, and system uptime encrypts it in the same wire format and posts it to the /api/c2/update endpoint on the C2 server.

Below table shows the C2 endpoints that the implant communicates:

Endpoint

Purpose

/api/c2/update

Reconnaissance beacon – victim system info

/api/c2/result

Command output exfiltration

/api/c2/screen

Screenshot upload

/api/c2/file_chunk

File exfiltration

/api/c2/rproxy_up

Reverse proxy upstream data

/api/c2/ws

Websocket – actor command channel

Every message on both channels, in both directions, uses the same symmetric encryption scheme. A hardcoded seed value stored in obfuscated form in the binary data section is decoded at startup and produces a 32-byte AES key.

Decoded AES seed: d791dd0ff3228ed29a8d7333d4567be829159c5632ea347780992006f91c5295 32-byte AES key: 4887AFC0A574E9419A9695EF083460F58E4EF9A1C40793523CE112251273BDF9

The C2 server then responds with an encrypted payload, whose inner map contains a command array identical in structure to those delivered over WebSocket. Commands received through HTTP are dispatched through the same logic. If the HTTP POST fails, the agent rotates to the next server address before retrying.

Figure 11. Snippet of NIK C2 implant’s C2 communication handler function.

The result transmission to the C2 is performed by the implant when a command handler completes its operation, the result is packaged into a response envelope containing the original command's identifier, the implant's own identifier, a type string formed by appending _response to the command name, the result data payload, and a top-level type marker of "result". This object is encrypted and delivered through either directly over the WebSocket connection if it is active, or via an HTTP POST to /api/c2/result.

Implant’s defense evasion and anti-analysis techniques

The NIK C2 implant deploys a layered set of defense evasion measures that activate immediately at startup and operate across the full compromise session. On launch, It hides its console window via API ShowWindow, renames the binary to “csrss.exe” in the Windows temp directory to impersonate a legitimate system process, disables Windows Recent Documents telemetry through a registry write action, and applies a critical-process flag via API NtSetInformationProcess with the parameter value 0x1D for ProcessBreakOnTermination that causes a Blue Screen of Death if any attempt is made to terminate the process through Task Manager or taskkill actions.

Figure 12. Snippet of NIK C2 implant’s evasion handler module.

Alongside these, two anti-debug checks IsDebuggerPresent and CheckRemoteDebuggerPresent run silently and call os.Exit(0) on detection, leaving no exception record or crash evidence. When directed by the C2, the implant can also escalate privileges without a UAC prompt using the fodhelper.exe COM hijack, which writes the implant path into HKCU\Software\Classes\ms-settings\Shell\Open\command, triggers elevation, and cleans the registry key within two seconds.

The implant bypasses the Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) by executing a hardcoded, embedded PowerShell script that patches memory inside “System.Management.Automation.dll”. Specifically, it overwrites the AmsiInitFailed field with a six-byte stub (MOV EAX, E_INVALIDARG; RET), forcing initialization to report failure and disabling content inspection for the remaining of the PowerShell session.

Figure 13. NIK C2 Implant’s AMSI bypass PowerShell script.

Conclusion

The emergence of NIK C2, an AI-enabled command-and-control framework, underscores a critical shift in modern malware design: the transition from static intrusion toolsets to dynamic, modular implants that adapt on demand. By embedding a live AI pipeline directly into the C2 loop, the compromised host is no longer a passive foothold but an autonomous operational asset. Operators can dynamically generate context-aware lure material, execute localized deception, synthesize operational intelligence, and craft targeted payloads directly on the compromised hosts — all while lowering the technical barrier which was traditionally required for such sophisticated tradecraft.

Coverage

The following ClamAV signature detects and blocks this threat:

Win.Trojan.GoDiscorder-10060526-0

articles.full_text:
Cisco Talos has identified UAT-11473, a highly sophisticated advanced persistent threat (APT) actor, who exploited CVE-2026-20127, an authentication bypass vulnerability in Cisco SD-WAN Catalyst Controller instances to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to affected systems.

UAT-11473 then installed a custom malware framework we track as “KeyDrift” consisting of multiple components geared towards collecting sensitive keying information, acting as backdoors and intermediate command-and-control (C2) hosts.

Observed targeting spans across space and satellite services, defense and aerospace technology, and policy research.

Talos assesses with high confidence that UAT-11473’s operating infrastructure overlaps considerably with Volt Typhoon’s “Silent Train” covert access network.

KeyDrift is a custom malware framework that is designed to operate in Cisco SD-WAN controller environments. Talos assesses with high confidence that the framework is designed to provide long-term persistent access and automated exfiltration of sensitive keying material. KeyDrift operates inside SD-WAN control-plane processes and is capable of intercepting decrypted control traffic, extracting control-session metadata and data-plane keying material, and staging or transmitting the collected material using encrypted records.

The framework's primary component is PolyFlame, a memory-resident module deployed through modified runit service paths. PolyFlame is injected into legitimate running vdaemon processes, and it can also masquerade as a packed “aaamgrd” loader variant. Once resident, PolyFlame interposes socket, DTLS, and runtime-linker behavior through functions such as recvfrom, sendto, getpeername, dlopen, dlsym, mprotect, and “/proc/%d/maps” parsing. This gives KeyDrift access to SD-WAN control-plane traffic from inside legitimate controller daemon execution rather than through a conventional endpoint beacon.

LittleFilch, another component of the KeyDrift framework, provides the collection and exfiltration capability identified in the framework. The module hooks “SSL_read” inside vdaemon, inspects decrypted control-plane buffers, extracts keying material for a list of predefined edge nodes, and stages the data locally in encrypted format for exfiltration.

Talos assesses with high confidence that KeyDrift's intended operational purpose is Cisco SD-WAN control-plane collection: persistent controller residence, in-band traffic access, key-material extraction from decrypted control messages, and encrypted staging or exfiltration of the recovered material. Observed variations of the KeyDrift modules and deployment mechanisms suggest active development of the framework’s capabilities.

KeyDrift analysis

KeyDrift uses Cisco SD-WAN runit service paths as its primary execution anchor. In the PolyFlame sshd deployment, the actor modifies the service run script, remounts /rootfs.rw executable, launches a malicious script “conf_sshd” in the background, and then starts the legitimate sshd service. The loader script enumerates running vdaemon PIDs, records them in “/tmp/system-vdaemon”, and invokes the injector component “rsshd” to inject PolyFlame (“libdssl.so”) into each process.

Recovered conf_sshd logic uses the same control flow across reviewed samples:

Figure 1. conf_sshd control flow logic.

Runit launchers

The observed sshd runit launcher preserves normal Cisco SD-WAN sshd startup logic while adding two malicious lines before service execution, which remount “/rootfs.rw” executable and background execution of conf_sshd, which then drives rsshd injection into vdaemon.

Figure 2. conf_sshd execution logic.

The recovered aaamgr runit launcher from an affected vBond appliance uses a parallel service-wrapper pattern, but it executes the packed aaamgrd PolyFlame loader directly. The deletion of the writable-overlay PAM configurations for sshd and login before remounting “/rootfs.rw” executable if part of the legitimate script, along with the invocation of the aaamgrd daemon via Python:

Figure 3. aamgrd daemon launch.

PolyFlame

PolyFlame is the primary operational module in the KeyDrift framework. PolyFlame operates at the socket and DTLS control-plane layer. PolyFlame serves two primary purposes:

Command execution via a TinyShell-styled backdoor

Intermediate C2 that can forward commands to and from the C2 to other peers

PolyFlame is primarily injected into the vdaemon process, providing operational obfuscation and access to all in-process state: DTLS session keys, vEdge topology, OMP routes, and policy tables. No hardcoded IPv4 addresses, binding ports, callback domains, URLs, host headers, or polling interval were recovered from the analyzed PolyFlame samples. PolyFlame is designed for in-band control or tasking over Cisco SD-WAN control-plane traffic rather than a conventional fixed external beacon.

This implant is meant to serve as a hook of the recvfrom() API call. The original recvfrom is replaced by a malicious subroutine in the vdaemon process. When recvfrom is called in the vdaemon process, the malicious subroutine will first execute the real/legitimate recvfrom() API to obtain the C2 IP address info for communicating with it in the future.

PolyFlame’s time check

The recvd data from the C2 consists of the MD5 value of a specific DATE. PolyFlame will calculate the local time on the device in format “%Y-%m-%d" and calculate its MD5 hash. If the MD5 calculated by the device does not match with the one sent by the C2, the implant will stop further execution. Otherwise, the implant then uses an “administrative code” from the C2 and performs an action.

PolyFlame’s tasking

PolyFlame contains an administrative mode that processes the admin code sent by the C2, that defines operations — it's one of the first flags checked in the backdoor:

Code = 1: Generate random bytes and send to C2. This is likely a check-in beacon or heartbeat for the C2.

Code = 2: Set implant type to backdoor (TinyShell) or intermediate C2.

Code = 3: Set up the command handler for the intermediate C2.

Any other code value: Check the implant type flag currently set. Based on the implant type flag, either send the accompanying data to TinyShell or the intermediate C2 component for processing.

PolyFlame’s command execution

PolyFlame contains a backdoor that matches the capabilities of TinyShell: file read, file write, and arbitrary command execution, but not interactive shell. This backdoor component’s implementation is quite similar to TinyShell, but the command codes differ. PolyFlame handles the following command codes:

Code = 0x100: Execute command using “/bin/sh -c <command>”

Code = 0x200: Write file to disk.

Code = 0x300: Read file from disk and send to the C2.

PolyFlame as an intermediate C2 component

The intermediate C2 component is a one-to-many handler (somewhat like a one-to-many multiplexer) — meaning the implant can connect to only one C2 but can connect to many peers who can be served by the intermediate C2 component. Similar to the TinyShell-backdoor component, the intermediate C2 component also accepts and processes specific command codes from the C2:

Code = 0x403: Create a thread to connect to the specified peer IP. Make a new connection and keep socket alive until specified.

Code = 0x404: Send data recvd from the C2 to a connected peer.

Code = 0x405: Remove a peer from the list of active connections.

Code = 0x407: Send a response recvd from a peer, back to the C2.

Code = 0x408: Set a specific value in memory.

PolyFlame variant: aaamgrd

Talos has observed a distinct PolyFlame variant that masquerades as the aaamgr service. The legitimate Cisco aaamgr component is a Python package; it does not normally appear as a compiled ELF runit service. This PolyFlame variant is executed by a malicious runit service under “/etc/sv/aaamgr/” with aaamgrd and a modified run launcher.

aaamgrd is a statically linked ELF64 executable with no section headers, a single RWE loader segment, and an RC4-encrypted embedded ELF payload. The loader uses direct syscalls including ptrace, fork, wait4, kill, tgkill, mmap, and mprotect. It performs an anti-debug check by deobfuscating /proc/%d/status and TracerPid: and exits if a tracer is present.

The observed staging sequence was:

Figure 4. PolyFlame staging sequence.

Note that in addition to the implant execution staging, there are also indications of timestomping.

LittleFilch: libcommon.so TLS interception module

LittleFilch is a control-session interception module positioned to collect data-plane keying material from control sessions visible to the injected vSmart process.

LittleFilch installs an SSL_read hook inside vdaemon. The hook calls the original SSL_read, then processes returned buffers only when the returned size is greater than 0x18F, the first decrypted byte is 0x07, and three marker patterns are checked for presence. These marker bytes are followed by the actual artifacts that LittleFilch aims to record:

LittleFilch records the extracted keying material and RSA-encrypts it before writing the output to “/var/tmp/vdaemon.bin”. It can then send the encrypted content over UDP in a DTLS 1.2 application-data style record.

Figure 5. Keying material recording format used by LittleFilch.

LittleFilch expects its configuration file — located at “/var/tmp/vdaemon.conf” — to contain two host port lines: one local bind IP/port and one remote destination IP/port. It deletes “/var/tmp/vdaemon.conf” after reading it. Talos has not been able to recover the “vdaemon.conf” file.

What does it mean to be "blue collar" for the blue team? Amy sat down with security researcher Ryan Fetterman to discuss his journey from federal agency work to his new role at Talos. He shares the realities of detection engineering — including the creative, often frustrating ways attackers evolve their tactics to stay one step ahead of traditional defenses.Beyond the technical grind, Ryan shares his philosophy on building a career in security without burning out. From the value of project-based learning to the importance of finding time to step away from the keyboard, here's Ryan's take on what it really means to navigate today's cybersecurity industry.

Amy Ciminnisi: Tell me a little bit about the journey that has taken you to Talos, from early on in your career through to now. How did you get here? I actually don't know that much about it.

Ryan Fetterman: I've been doing security about 15 years now, and my career was largely shaped by where I started in the DC area. I spent about a decade there. I started out in consulting and then pivoted over to research, but that was a great place to get started.

I got a lot of great experience in federal agencies and government consulting, continued my education down there, got trained up, got certifications and things like that. And that was where I got my first exposure to doing actual security operations, which is what I really stuck with. It was my first exposure to Splunk.

Querying lots of log data and building visualizations and analytics in Splunk was the first time in my career that I felt it was kind of my natural inclination. It seems like it should have been more obvious to me looking back on it, but it's something that I try to explain to people a lot. When you first get into security, there's a desire to kind of find your specialization and start working towards it. But in my experience, it's just not something that you can rush.

I met the people connected with that space, which eventually led to me going to work for Splunk. I worked on the Splunk research team, SURGe. And then after the Cisco acquisition of Splunk, I ultimately became reorganized into Talos.

AC: I'm sure there have been so many challenges, so many obstacles in your way as you're trying to do this research. Can you share one that you've faced and how it shaped your perspective on cybersecurity?

RF: Something that stuck with me was actually my first advanced persistent threat (APT) incident. Now, you can look this up. It's called Pandora Song if you search for the C2. I was in the DC area working in a federal SOC, and I was doing some of the first host-based analytics at the time, which have now become kind of the concentration of a lot of detection. Engineering and analytics are host-based, so this was kind of pioneering at the time.

I was looking at a lot of host-based sensors and writing analytics in Splunk, actually, and we had been tipped off to this incident by a third party. I was looking through the details of the incident and how the attacker was carrying out the progression of their attack...

Want to see more? Watch the full interview, and don’t forget to subscribe to our YouTube channel for future episodes of Humans of Talos.

Welcome to this week’s edition of the Threat Source newsletter.

Here for the latest on the PHP vulnerabilities? Head on down to ‘The One Big Thing’. Talos has published a blog to explain what we know so far, and details the Snort coverage available, including rules in the Community Ruleset.

But if you want a bit of levity, here’s what I wrote before everything kicked off yesterday:

Ever feel like the world is moving too fast to keep up? Well, I bring you scientific proof that it’s not just you.

For millions of years, the moon has been slowing down the Earth’s rotation. But over the past decade, we’ve been speeding up (I KNEW I was aging faster than before). Apparently, changes in the Earth’s core are involved (either that, or the 1978 Superman film was a documentary).

This is all causing massive headaches for the people responsible for keeping time. They’re officially called “The International Bureau of Weights and Measures”, but I’m going to call them “The Time-Keepers”. For nerd reasons).

The issue is that the atomic clocks that power so many of our systems, and the rotation of our planet, don’t always agree. Atomic clocks keep extremely consistent time, while each Earth day is rarely the same length as the next. Atomic timekeeping absolutely cannot stand that level of flexibility (have a watch of our “The Light We Keep” documentary to see the importance that accurate clocks have on critical infrastructure).

To keep Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), which is based on atomic clocks, aligned with Earth’s rotation, we introduced a “leap second” in 1972. This system allows for an extra second to be added, or taken away, when we stray too far from atomic time.

A few days ago, The Time-Keepers voted to officially abolish the leap second. Why? Well, there’s a few parts to it.

For the past 54 years, we’ve never once had a second removed from our lives. They’ve always been added (27 of them to be precise). I myself have experienced 20 of these extra seconds. If I’d have known that, I’d have used them more wisely. Like thinking before saying, “Love you too!” to the post-person this morning.

That added time, while it seems nice to have on the surface, can wreak havoc with our modern technology systems. In 2012, the extra second caused so much confusion that it crashed Reddit, among other systems.

The recent speeding-up of the Earth’s rotation complicates things further. If we keep going at this rate, it could result in the world’s first ever “negative second”. If you thought our technology systems struggled with added time, there are a lot of sciency brains who are very worried about the impact of taking time away. One of those concerns being… it’s never been done before.

So, what’s The Time-Keeper’s solution? Invent more time! Woooo.

Starting next May, the leap second will be replaced with a "leap hour," allowing UTC to diverge from Earth's rotation by up to an hour before a correction is made. None of us will get to experience that extra hour in our lifetimes, but our Great, Great, Great, Great, Great, Great, Great, Great, Great, Great, Great grandchildren are going to have one hell of a party.

For us current mortals, we’re all getting a little less time, and we’re hurtling through space a little faster. Happy Thursday!

But I guess I do want to make the point that I’m glad the risk has been thoroughly assessed ahead of, ahem, time. The Time-Keepers have decided that the world’s infrastructure should not have to find out how it handles a missing second by collectively experiencing one.

And I don’t even want to think about how all the AIs would cope with a negative second…

There’s something here for incident response planning. “It’s never happened before” is an excellent reason to test whether you’re ready for it. Run the exercise. Find out which part of your plan depends on something that, in this scenario, is also broken. Preferably before an adversary gets to supervise the practical demonstration.

Now, if only the Time-Keepers can abolish Daylight Savings Time next...

The one big thing

Two unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) flaws were discovered in PHP, rocking the internet. Dubbed "php2shell" and triggered by a simple HTTP request, this vulnerability affects every build since 5.4. Talos assesses that all industries running PHP applications are at risk for exploitation if systems remain unpatched.

Why do I care?

PHP runs WordPress, Drupal, Magento, Shopware, WooCommerce, and many other ubiquitous internet staples, so the possible blast radius is enormous. Older branches are end of life (EOL) and will not receive patches; these could account for around 50% of use cases.

So now what?

Cisco customers are covered with the Cisco Talos Network Intrusion Prevention (SNORT®) signatures 67359 and 67360. If your organization is running PHP 8.1 or older, Talos very strongly advises immediate update to PHP 8.2 or later. There is no patch for PHP 8.1 or older. See the article for more specific coverage and detection guidance.

See an interview with Nick Biasini on php2shell defense:

Cisco Talos observed abuse of more than 25 legitimate platforms over the past year, exploiting the built-in trust of collaboration, file-sharing, payment and other services to reach their targets.

There's only so much code: the rise in vulnerability numbersThe September Microsoft Patch Tuesday release included 975 vulnerability advisories. This month, 1,415 vulnerabilities were just dropped. Compared to a pre-June average of 100 a month, that increase is staggering. Where did they come from? And what does the future look like?

Update 10/22: Added section detailing observations of in the wild exploitation and associated IOCs.

Cisco Talos is tracking the disclosure of two unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) flaws in PHP core, dubbed “php2shell”, triggered by a plain HTTP request and exploitable before any application code runs, affecting every PHP build since 5.4. Based on the entities involved in the disclosure, artificial intelligence and associated technologies played a key role in the discovery of these vulnerabilities — yet another example of how these technologies are forcing change across the landscape, most notably on patching processes for organizations because of the wave of vulnerabilities being disclosed.

Cisco customers are covered with the Cisco Talos Network Intrusion Prevention (SNORT®) signatures 67359, 67360, and 67375. These rules are also available in the Community Ruleset for open-source customers. Splunk Enterprise Security customers have an Enterprise Security Content Update with detections available. Please refer to the following recommendations, detection, and coverage guidance for more information.

Details

CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are both critical vulnerabilities with a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2.

CVE-2026-109618 occurs when out-of-memory handling interrupts PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized. Request cleanup may then treat invalid data as valid.

CVE-2026-109619 occurs when a stale internal state is reused after its backing memory has already been freed, before normal initialization resets it.

Impact

The potential blast radius is enormous and extends across the PHP ecosystem. The vulnerability sits in PHP core, so applications running affected versions — including WordPress, Drupal, Magento, Shopware, WooCommerce, and Laravel, plus PHP sites hosted through cPanel or Plesk — may be exposed. Note that many older branches will no longer receive fixes, so customers are urged to upgrade to a supported version as soon as possible.

Talos regularly investigates threat actor exploitation of vulnerabilities. State-sponsored and affiliated threat actors, as well as ransomware and other financially motivated groups, all employ tactics to exploit RCE. Talos assesses that all industries running PHP applications are at risk for exploitation if systems remain unpatched.

PHP 8.1 and older are end of life (EOL), and PHP 8.2 security support ends Dec. 31, 2026. Talos’ initial estimates based on open-source intelligence show a significant corpus of PHP systems that will not receive a patch (~50%). If your organization is running PHP 8.1 or older, Talos very strongly advises immediate update to PHP 8.2 or later. There is no patch for PHP 8.1 or older.

Talos is actively monitoring the impact of these CVEs and has not seen them being exploited in the wild yet (as of October 21, 2026 14:00 UTC/10:00 a.m. ET).

Observed Exploitation

Cisco Talos began observing exploitation attempts within hours of the vulnerabilities’ disclosure. So far, most of the activity is scanning, along with some uncoordinated attempts to deliver various payloads. This is expected: scanning or basic exploitation with public proof-of-concept (PoC) code takes far less effort than integrating a vulnerability into an actor’s own tooling. We expect exploitation volume to grow in the coming days, and campaigns to become more sophisticated and coordinated as more capable groups finish updating their tooling and begin deploying it.

Recommendations and detection guidance

Talos strongly recommends all PHP users to upgrade to the available fixed releases. There are no intermediate or temporary controls that provide comprehensive protection; however, PHP advises that the following measure may reduce exposure to specific attack paths:

CVE-2026-109618

Set memory_limit=-1, preferably in a way applications can't override, such as php_admin_value in the FPM pool or Apache configuration, and check that no pool, directory or application setting puts a finite limit back. This removes the controllable PHP memory limit failure, but an underlying allocation failure can still reach the vulnerable path.

Set a low post_max_size. For applications that don't require file uploads, set post_max_size = 8M. If file uploads are necessary, set post_max_size = 32M. Keep upload_max_filesize below post_max_size. Consider enforcing limits at the web server or proxy level for decoded request size, input field count, multipart part count, header count, and nesting depth. These limits must also cover requests without a usable Content-Length.

Use a container or cgroup limit as an availability boundary, preferably with a policy that kills only the affected worker. Do not substitute RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, as these can cause the vulnerable allocation failure.

CVE-2026-109619

Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and restart every worker. Use php.ini, an FPM pool, or server configuration that applies before request parsing. Do not rely on ini_set() or FPM .user.ini. This blocks the confirmed session paths but not other variants.

On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0 and restart every worker. This blocks the confirmed fatal backtrace path only.

Remove invalid or deprecated settings applied per request that emit diagnostics before initialization. Hiding diagnostics with error_reporting, display_errors, or @ does not help.

Fix attacker-reachable fatal errors and execution timeouts, including failures in callbacks, upload or import processing, and cleanup.

This is another vulnerability that owes its discovery to AI and its associated technologies. As we move through 2026, the wave of vulnerabilities and related patches is building. Talos advises organizations to work on a triaged process for prioritizing vulnerabilities with a specific focus on public-facing systems and vulnerabilities that are under active exploitation. The glaring need to prioritize vulnerabilities along with a streamlined process for rolling out patching strongly indicates that the historic trend of “baking in” patches before deployment is not going to survive the AI era.

The true impact of this vulnerability will take time to evaluate. These types of vulnerabilities that impact core technologies tend to cascade into other platforms and applications as they evaluate impact and provide associated patching, harkening back to the waves of exploitation that we saw after Log4J.

Coverage

SNORT® SIDs covering these vulnerabilities for subscribers: 67359, 67360, 67375. Free community rules are live through our Community Ruleset.

Splunk has released an Enterprise Security Content Update (ESCU) related to the ongoing PHP2Shell activity with additional detections. Splunk Enterprise Security customers are urged to download and apply.

Talos would like to highlight the efforts of Ankur Tyagi, Dalton Schaadt, Brandon Stultz, and Matt Killion for providing emergency coverage and mitigations for these threats.

In this video, Talos’ Nick Biasini explains what the vulnerabilities allow adversaries to do, how to assess your exposure, and what defenders should prioritize.

Amy Ciminnisi 0:00

Welcome to the Talos Takes Podcast, where we discuss Talos' latest research and security news. This podcast is for everyone, from the C-suite to the front lines.

Amy Ciminnisi 0:12

Welcome to the special Cybersecurity Awareness Month edition of Talos Takes. Last week we talked with Martin Lee on AI honeypots and various impediments you can deploy to stop an adversary in their tracks or make their life a living hell, whichever.

Amy Ciminnisi 0:30

But today we're talking about one of the holy grails of security architecture, network segmentation. We all know that limiting an attacker's movement in your network is critical, but moving from theory to reality there is where things start to get complicated.

Amy Ciminnisi 0:47

I am joined by Craig Jackson from Talos IR today to talk about how to move past these definitions, identify practical starting points for your team, and turn segmentation into a tool not just for prevention, but also for incident response. We'll also be touching on an emerging topic that is gaining steam, AI kill switches. Craig, how are you doing?

Craig Jackson 1:11

I'm well, Amy, how are you today?

Amy Ciminnisi 1:13

Doing pretty well. Recovering from a cold, but we're making it work.

Craig Jackson 1:18

You couldn't tell. I mean, your voice sounds perfectly fine to me.

Amy Ciminnisi 1:21

Thank you so much. Appreciate that.

Amy Ciminnisi 1:24

So this is a really cool topic. And I think as someone who is newer to cybersecurity, it seems like the word segmentation is everywhere. People are throwing it around. Um, but there are varying degrees of segmentation, right? So you have your network VLANs on one end, you have micro-segmentation on the other. Um, how do you identify which approach is going to work for your team?

Craig Jackson 1:50

That's a great question. And it's it's one that is going to vary by organization. So when whenever we talk about controlled deployment from a proactive or preventive perspective, we don't just want to recommend, you know, bias, you know, creating a bunch of budget, buying a bunch of tools that look really cool, and then just kind of like throwing them haphazardly into the environment.

Amy Ciminnisi 2:14

Yeah.

Craig Jackson 2:14

You always want to start out with foundational practices like threat modeling, risk assessment, um, asset management, which I talk about asset management more now as an incident responder than I have in the past as sort of a security analyst um or an auditor because it's so critical to understand where things are.

Craig Jackson 2:36

So once you have that understanding, that preliminary understanding of what's in the environment, where it is, what needs to be to have the most protections afforded it, then you can start laying out, okay, we need network segmentation at this point, or we've got a cloud control over here. So we need to have workflow segmentation or or micro segmentation here. Mapping out that sort of understanding will give you the most effective approach to what type of segmentation needs to be layered and where to fully implement that as a effective control.

Amy Ciminnisi 3:12

Right. And as an incident responder yourself, um, you know that segmentation is a really great preventative control, but it's also really useful for response when you're mid-breach. Um, how should teams be planning for segmentation um to contain a threat and you know, not just a way to design a network?

Craig Jackson 3:38

Yeah, that gets into the discussion of something that I like to call immediate containment actions. So when when we come into an emergency response situation where there's an investigation taking place because of a security incident or a suspected security incident, you don't necessarily want to wait until you're so far through the incident response life cycle that you're at a point of, okay, now we have we're comfortable with with what's going on, we understand what's happening, let's put our containment in now.

Craig Jackson 4:08

Typically, there's going to be that immediate containment, like, hey, we see these five systems are exhibiting this indicator of compromise or this type of suspicious activity. Let's isolate them, let's let's you know get them off of the production network so we can investigate what's going on there. So preparing for that immediate containment action and being able to implement those types of things is is critical. And it's not always easy because if your immediate containment action is something like let's disconnect from the internet or let's shut down an entire segment of virtual machines or virtual servers, there's going to be some definite operational impact to that type of approach. So planning for the segmentation, it's really important to make sure that you're looking forward to understanding what those impacts could be, where you might be able to implement that segmentation as an immediate containment action and understand who has the authority and the process to put those that segmentation in place.

Craig Jackson 5:19

I will add that um when it comes to segmentation in turn and immediate containment in terms of tiers, we we recommend kind of like a red, yellow, green tiering for our network segments when we're trying to respond and recover from a security incident. And it it can help an organization, either visually or conceptually, to structure that as you know, your red segment is known compromised or high confidence compromised systems that you don't want touching anything else. So you you kind of put those all in a specific segment. Um, from a yellow perspective, you looked at that as maybe these are systems that are remediated, but you still want to keep an eye on them to make sure that that your remediation is effective and that the adversary hasn't left any persistence or anything like that happening on the system. And then your green segment would be your production environment.

Craig Jackson 6:14

And every organization is going to have their own way of approaching this. But the idea here is you're using your segmentation throughout the incident response and recovery process to make sure that the adversary isn't able to, or the malware, whatever is the situation you're dealing with, isn't able to compromise or re-infect those systems. So again, it's it sounds like it it could be an something arduous to put in place or an arduous approach to take, but the organizations that take the time to lay out and map out that type of segmentation, either at the network level, at the host level, at the process or application level, are the ones that are going to naturally be able to put it in play uh more efficiently and more effectively during an incident.

Amy Ciminnisi 7:01

Yeah. And honestly, um, one of the biggest hurdles that I constantly hear from uh guests on the show is visibility and that you you can't segment what you don't understand. And so how do teams tackle this? You know, especially ones that may have inherited um systems from previous employees, they're plopped down in the middle of nowhere. Um, how how do you tackle this discovery phase? It sounds so difficult.

Craig Jackson 7:32

Yeah. Have I have I mentioned asset management and asset inventories before?

Amy Ciminnisi 7:37

I think so, maybe once or twice.

Craig Jackson 7:39

Yeah, yeah. I always feel like the least popular person in the room. I mean, you can actually see people's expressions just like sour towards me when I bring this up when I, you know, public speaking and stuff.

Amy Ciminnisi 7:50

It's the boring stuff that makes a difference.

Craig Jackson 7:52

That's true, it's true. And it, you know, it it it applies here as well. So historically, there's a manual approach to this. I mean, you could theoretically use things like Wireshark or TCP dump or you know, a couple other, I suppose, freeware utilities to try to map out traffic flows. But you know, nowadays there's all kinds of commercial applications that will really accelerate an organization's ability to understand what traffic is going where, traffic volumes, you know, establishing network baselines and things like that. Um you know, being Cisco, I sort of think of secure network analytics, I think of like Thousand Eyes, but you know, there's other many other commercial utilities out there and commercial tools that that organizations can drop into place. And and that that's really what you would probably want to use to try to identify this. And I I use the term baseline to step and go, and that's another important thing, especially as we look at the potential for data exfiltration during incidents or getting into agentic malware and some some AI-enabled attacks, if we're seeing gigantic spikes in traffic volumes and things like that, you want to be able to detect those types of anomalies, both in the directionality of traffic as well as in fluctuations in traffic volume.

Amy Ciminnisi 9:16

So micro-segmentation is notoriously pretty difficult, right? Um, and so if if a team realizes that that just isn't possible today for them to do, they just don't have the capacity, what should they prioritize first? Is there, you know, low-hanging fruit that can give them a bigger boost to their posture, or what what suggestions would you have?

Craig Jackson 9:41

I would propose that that would vary by organization. And I want to be careful not to make general statements because you know, if I just say, like, hey, this application server or this file server, you know, make sure you understand traffic flows from here and segmentation around these, that might do a disservice to other organizations where that's not as much of a priority. So I mentioned before some of the early steps for understanding the security implications in your environment, like threat modeling, uh, risk assessment, security control assessment, data criticality mapping, all that kind of stuff. That is going to give you a strong foundation to understanding where you need to put protections in place, such as segmentation and micro-segmentation.

Craig Jackson 10:27

And you also, as an organization, likely want to consider regulatory and contractual requirements as well, because there are certain um, you know, regulatory security frameworks that are going to actually stipulate, hey, you need to have segmentation in place, and it it should probably look something like this. It's not going to be granular, you know, it'd say specifically around application servers or domain controllers, things like that, but it's definitely going to say you have to have network controls and segmentation in place around this type of system at this point, you know.

Amy Ciminnisi 11:05

So let's move on to a topic that is tangentially related, uh, but that you've mentioned that you're hearing a lot of buzz from uh customers about, and then also on online forums, things like that. Um, we're seeing a lot of interest in AI kill switches. You describe this as controls designed to quickly contain or stop AI-enabled adversaries, um, or even legitimate AI applications that start behaving erratically. Um, let's uh talk a little bit more about this.

Craig Jackson 11:43

Yeah, so this is a topic that over the course of the past few months, more and more of our customers seem to be bringing up. And you know, at first it was kind of like, oh, this is that's unique. Haven't really thought about that before. As as we continue to move further and further into the AI era, I guess it's gonna be coming more and more more and more commonplace to talk about this. But um, this is something that we we've seen increasing interest in. And it it kind of gets phrased, and maybe I'm biased as an instant responder and a threat intelligence professional, but you know, it kind of gets phrased around something like an immediate containment action, where a few different circumstances or scenarios you might consider would be, you know, a threat actor dropping agentic AI malware in the environment or a uh malware that is AI augmented, I guess I could say. You could see, you know, an AI application that is either developed by the organization or is has been contracted by a third party and is used in the environment, maybe exceeding its access or going places or doing things that it's not necessarily supposed to be doing by default.

Craig Jackson 12:54

And the concept around all that is since these applications and this malware is potentially moving at machine speed, how do you get out in front of it quickly and implement that that kill switch or implement that containment action? Because with a with a human speed attack, hands-on keyboard, you know, human threat actor, you've got maybe a little bit more of a window to drop an immediate containment action in place to kind of halt the progress of the adversary in the environment. At machine speed, your your window is a lot more narrow for making yeah, you're you're you've got to do that a lot more quickly, and you've you've got to be arguably more confident that when you implement that, it's going to be effective because second chances are going to be probably few and far between.

Craig Jackson 13:41

So that's kind of where our customers are and and some of the organizations that we work with are going with that particular topic is exploring this in advance because it is still such a nascent idea in terms of you know putting these types of controls in place for AI, uh, and then understanding, you know, or or maybe mapping out and documenting what their internal approach would be to implementing those AI kill switches.

Amy Ciminnisi 14:13

I'm I'm curious, would like strong segmentation kind of widen that time uh that that gap up enough for um defenders to be able to deploy a kill switch more? Like I'm thinking about like you were talking about the speed of agentic malware or things like that. Like how how does segmentation come into play here?

Craig Jackson 14:39

It certainly could. The challenge there is it's tough to answer that unless we are we're saying, okay, are we talking exclusively about network-level segmentation? Are we talking about host-based isolation, which is, you know, again, kind of a form of one-off segmentation? Um, or are we talking about something at the application or workflow level? So it's it's certainly possible and and likely that segmentation could impede an an AI augmented attack, but the question is for how long? Um, you know, if you're not necessarily directly addressing the AI component of that attack, how long will your other compensating controls remain in place and remain effective before that that pseudo autonomous malware or or threat actor is able to circumvent or bypass or or overcome that particular control?

Amy Ciminnisi 15:38

And then also let's maybe talk about the like the collateral impacts too. Like you said, second chances could be few and far in between. And you know, you really want to make sure that the switch is doing what you want it to do. Um, so like if you are talking about this as, you know, an immediate containment act, what are these collateral impacts that people need to consider?

Craig Jackson 16:04

I think they'll probably be similar to what we would see with an immediate containment action. And, you know, I alluded to two examples earlier. I think shutting down or heavily segmenting an entire server network uh you know or VM infrastructure to protect it from an attack, and also disconnecting from the internet, which is something that we see organizations either considering or in some cases actually going through with just completely severing all ties to the internet. Those are going to come with operational impacts, both internally, and if you're you have customers, if you have vendor partners, things like that that that need access to your resources, there's going to be an impact there as well. And also, people are probably going to take notice in the news media and you know, in the public that hey, this this entire company's infrastructure suddenly is offline. So um, there's different levels of impact, both operationally and reputationally, there that need to be considered.

Craig Jackson 17:01

The same is probably going to be true of an AI kill switch eventually. As AI applications become more prevalent in the operational environment for enterprise organizations, as more and more applications become dependent upon AI workflows and processes, dropping a kill switch into place, just like I alluded to with a with an immediate containment action, is probably going to have similar outcomes where there's going to be an operational impact in the organization and potential reputational damage from people sitting up and taking notice that something weird is going on as well. So, you know, I would argue that some of the things that we're discussing with customers right now and and should be considered as we continue to work fully work through maturing AI kill switches is you know, what are the the best locations in the environment to deploy them? Uh, do additional tools need to be deployed, or can we leverage existing security controls as part of that effort? Um, who has the authority? Just like with an immediate containment action, who has the authority to activate a kill switch? And are there thresholds that need to be met before that type of action is considered as a security measure? Um we already talked about operational impact, and then documenting all of this as part of your IRP, testing it, making sure that it's just it's not metaphorically sort of shooting from the hip, if you will, um, with your with your security controls, making sure that the team understands how to use them, what they're for, how to implement them, and and what that authority and that potential impact might be from deploying them.

Amy Ciminnisi 18:48

The former tech writer in me was so excited when you said documentation. And also just like looking at all the incident response plans that I get my eyes on day to day. Like, if this is something that is newer to your organization and you're considering putting something like this into place, like don't wait to get documentation down for all of those things that you said.

Craig Jackson 19:13

It makes a difference. It makes it we see it in in our investigations and our emergency response engagements. We see it in tabletop exercises. It's very clear when you sit down with a customer for a TTX and you ask a question, let's say it's about immediate containment actions or AI kill switches or any type of defensive measure like that, it's very clear which organizations have it documented, they know where to find that IRP, and they just spell it out for you immediately versus those that maybe struggle with it a little bit more. Or it's maybe it's more clear that it's an ad hoc process that that isn't broadly understood across the organization.

Amy Ciminnisi 19:54

Any any final words of wisdom for our listeners?

Craig Jackson 19:57

Oh man, I didn't know there was gonna be a words of wisdom question. No, I mean I could I'm sure I could go off one wild tangents about things that we're seeing across the threat landscape right now, but I think preparation, take your preparation steps, don't wait until it's actually happening and you're in the midst of an incident to figure this stuff out.

Amy Ciminnisi 20:14

Well, thanks so much for coming on today, Craig. Really appreciate it.

Craig Jackson 20:17

Thank you, Amy. Appreciate it as well.

Amy Ciminnisi 20:19

Yeah. Thank you so much for listening, everyone. We have a ton of Cybersecurity Awareness Month content out and even more headed your way. So check out our blog, blog.talosintelligence.com, for our latest posts. Stay safe out there.

articles.title: There's only so much code: the rise in vulnerability numbers
articles.context: Despite a 105% year-over-year surge in CVEs, Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEVs) grew by only 37%, and only 3 of September's 975 Microsoft advisories saw in-the-wild...
articles.full_text:
Frontier AI models (like Mythos) are rapidly mining decades of technical debt across ubiquitous legacy libraries, driving monthly Microsoft Patch Tuesday vulnerability advisories up more than tenfold (reaching 1,415 this month). This volume is overwhelming open-source maintainers and putting pressure on the traditional 90-day coordinated disclosure model.

Despite a 105% year-over-year surge in CVEs, Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEVs) grew by only 37%, and only 3 of September's 975 Microsoft advisories saw in-the-wild exploitation, demonstrating that the vast majority of AI-discovered bugs are not practically exploited.

We may be able to take new-bug-class vulnerability spikes as evidence that these vulnerabilities will eventually level off and decline, once the historical code backlog is remediated and AI verification is embedded directly into new development pipelines.

With attackers able to parse patches faster via AI, defenders cannot cover for all possible threats. Organizations should continue to build robust defense-in-depth. Prioritize high-exploitability flaws in their specific environments, implement interim mitigations (such as LiveProtect), deploy behavioral anomaly detection, and integrate current AI evaluation models into their software build chains.

The September Microsoft Tuesday release included 975 vulnerability advisories. This month, 1,415 vulnerabilities were just dropped. Compared to a pre-June average of 100 a month, that increase is staggering. Where did they come from?

As of April, frontier models came onto the scene more fine-tuned than ever toward vulnerability detection, particularly with the introduction of Mythos. The deluge brings a lot of questions:

If these numbers are real, why hasn’t the internet collapsed?

Are these vulnerabilities a new breed, and if not, why didn’t analysts find them in code that is sometimes decades old?

Is the coordinated disclosure model still relevant in an era of this kind of speed?

How in the world do defenders deal with those numbers?

Should we go home, kiss our spouses, and prepare for the end?

The answer to many of these questions boils down to this: The majority of these vulnerabilities are coming from repositories of old code from large-profile products and systems; and disclosure does not equal weaponization.

Where is it from?

AI is chewing through a backlog of technical debt in libraries and tools used as the dependable, best-practice lynchpins of so many environments. These models have a new perspective, an ability to "think" without some of the hangups or assumptions of human defenders, and they are thorough in listing those vulnerabilities.

Entrenched older tools have always been prime targets because of their predictability; attackers know those tools and all their secrets, and they know what is likely to be present in a network with them. Multi-exploit attacks can be deployed with little variability.

Pre-Mythos threat actors exploited log4j (CVE-2021-44228) to immense success. The library was ubiquitous, included in nearly every environment, but not a component that got cataloged in visibility scans. A combination of scale and low visibility meant defenders were blindsided, scrambling to find out if they even used the log4j library before starting to concoct a mitigation plan.

Talos has ongoing relationships with some of the largest technical vendors (such as the Microsoft Active Protections Process (MAPP) agreement). Organizations share additional information—detection guidance or maybe a POC — for vulnerabilities that are most likely to be exploited, to enable Talos to provide adequate coverage when the advisories are announced. "Microsoft believes it is important for us to provide detection content, based on their guidance," as Yves Younan, Director of Talos Vulnerability Discovery, Detection, and Testing, says.

Talos has needed to invest more resources to get coverage in on time for critical vendors like Microsoft to keep up with notifications coming in fast and often on staggered or out-of-band timelines.

For larger vendors, the pressure is handleable for now. However, open-source projects are getting flooded. Some projects have a trusted group that can combine to tackle patches, and some share with the full community for immediate assistance, but it is up to the project. The internet runs on open-source work.

The pace of discovery presents a challenge for the traditional coordinated disclosure system vulnerability hunters have been using for years, and some are calling it into question.

Security vulnerabilities should be reported, to enable an informed defender base and regular patching, and vendors responsible for vulnerable code need time to create coverage. A timed disclosure model where notifications are sent to a vendor, who then has a set period of time (typically 90 days) to provide coverage before the disclosure is released publicly, has created a more secure online environment for decades.

Now, many practitioners are releasing advisories publicly without a disclosure period beforehand. The reasoning is that if one AI can find a weakness, any other could, so the vulnerability is already, effectively, released.

This conversation is actively changing expectations around vulnerability disclosure, and guidance is in flux.

Will it stay this high?

No one knows the future, but we can always look to the past for insight.

Numbers of vulnerabilities jump drastically when a new bug class is identified, as their possibilities are explored to the fullest. Then the discoveries plateau and drop off.

When format string vulnerabilities were discovered as a new bug class in 2000, the initial influx of discoveries ramped up and up, until reaching a peak in 2005 and then slowly declining over the next couple of years. Format string vulnerabilities are still discovered, but they are a smaller overall fraction of the number of CVEs discovered in a year.

Theoretically, AI-assisted vulnerability discovery could go the same way.

While frontier models have not discovered a new vulnerability class, they are more efficient at discovering known types of software vulnerabilities. Given that a lot of vital software has a long history of code releases, there’s plenty of code to mine for weaknesses. But there’s only so much code… right?

Old and commonly used tools are often under the highest scrutiny, lending them one kind of safety: Because of their popularity, utility, and stability, when popular tools have vulnerabilities, they are discovered fast and patched promptly.

As the historical backlog of essential systems is turned over by AI, vulnerabilities will be found and patched. New code will ideally be run through AI bug-checkers that will prevent new vulnerabilities from being introduced. The rate of new vulns should level off and drop accordingly.

There are some caveats. In the past, as vulnerability disclosures increased through coordinated disclosures, we saw increased adoption of mitigations. Exploitation became significantly harder. Attackers often need to chain together 3 or more vulnerabilities to successfully exploit a system.

However, more awareness of vulnerabilities often leads to more exploitation. Attackers often use vendor patches meant to protect customers to discover where vulnerabilities might exist. The frequency of patching has delayed human attackers via parsing bottlenecks, but AI can eliminate that problem.

Are the numbers the real issue?

The volume is certainly up.

Fresh as this blog is being finished, the October Patch Tuesday dropped almost 500 more than last month.

With refinement, any vulnerability could become a link to a path of effect. But... not all vulnerabilities are exploitable. Some are wildly impractical for attacker use. In fact, the percent of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEVs) is vastly smaller than the found vulnerabilities.

Of the 975 vulnerabilities Microsoft reported in September, there were only three in-the-wild exploits detected. When viewed by percentage, vulnerabilities versus KEVs tell a different and perhaps reassuring story.

Compared with the same period last year, additions to the known-exploited vulnerability list increased by 37%, while published CVEs increased by 105%. However, we wouldn't necessarily expect those figures to grow in proportion. Adversaries only need enough useful vulnerabilities to compromise their targets, and the same vulnerabilities can be reused against many organizations. The KEV count tracks distinct vulnerabilities known to be exploited, not the number of attacks or successful compromises.

AI helps ingest code, advisory reports, and attack surfaces with inhuman speed, but it cannot currently make judgment calls about the value of a weakness.

For defenders, the question remains the same: Which vulnerabilities provide a viable path into their environment, and how do you close those paths?

What do we do now?

The undeniable danger here is in exploitation time going down rapidly, while the vulnerabilities that could become exploits is still going up. The biggest hurdle for a defender is determining what is a real vulnerability for their environment, and what is not.

Different defenders have different forms of control depending on their role.

For those who are writing code, the new standard validation chain should include AI evaluation by models at least as up to date as those being used to hunt for vulnerabilities. It is relatively cheap to run new code through AI, but very expensive to run a cumbersome backlog of old code through. Bite it off in chunks.

For those whose role involves keeping the tools ready: Upgrade ASAP. Don't stop there.

For Cisco customers, implement LiveProtect to mitigate vulnerabilities between advisory release day and patching, to give time for that patching. Do this for everything you own.

Move beyond static domain blocking and implement behavioral detection that alerts on anomalous traffic patterns directed toward automation platforms.

Hone your focus to the vulnerabilities with the highest exploitability in your environment. KEVs are far less common among the sea of advisories, and their numbers have not risen proportionally with the AI-assisted deluge.

Focus on building defense-in-depth. Employ multiple protection systems, to cover for delays in patching. Implement interim mitigations (such as LiveProtect), create custom IPS/Snort triggers to block pre-patched traffic using SnortML, deploy behavioral anomaly detection, and integrate current AI evaluation models in software build chains.

Dive deeper into this conversation with the latest TTP interview with Yves Younan and vulnerability researcher Bella Fusari.

For more numbers and advice for defenders:

Don't swing at everything

articles.title: The Q3 Vulnerability Pulse: Discovery ≠ Exploitation
articles.context: (Hack Read) Ivanti zero-day chain gave attackers root access to fully patched VPN CVE-2026-104935 affects Ivanti Connect Secure and it can be exploited for unauthenticated...
articles.full_text:
Welcome to this week’s edition of the Threat Source newsletter.

I've been following a lot of (sometimes heated) threads and discussions lately about the current vulnerability landscape. I learned new words/phrases such as Summer of Hell (although I'm writing this with 1°C/34°F outside), Vulnpocalypse, Bugmageddon, Bugpocalypse, Breachpocalypse...

Let's look at some numbers:

We crossed the 70k mark, and it's only the end of September. This has never been seen before — I think we can agree this number is skyrocketing. Also, CVE numbering organically grew into the six-digit range. Check your tooling. Some might say we broke that barrier already in 2014 (CVE-2014-125110), or even hit seven digits in 2015 (CVE-2015-1000013), but those were allocated artificially. (History note: Before 2014, 9999 was the highest possible identifier.)

So that could be seen as the apocalypse argument. On the other hand, we have the KEV numbers:

They didn't explode... yet? Counting by sheer volume, YoY, CVEs increased by 105%, while KEV only grew 37%. Sounds huge at first, but following a 30% increase from 2024 to 2025, that's less dramatic — a counter-argument of sorts.

CVEs from 2025 or older still account for 33%. In other words, a good third of the KEVs are suggesting there is a patch gap. Looking at the 2026 CVEs, the share where the publication date matches the date added to KEV is 29%, which is only 2% more than (all of) 2025. Acknowledging this "math" is not the whole ball of wax, but it still tells me we are not living in a zero-day apocalypse right now. There’s also a slight uptick in networking gear-related CVEs, to 27%.

This is the second time I'll ask you to check your tooling. A new column, “forensicTriage,” was added to the KEV to flag which high-risk vulnerabilities require mandatory forensic triage and incident response workflows. You can read more about it in BOD 26-04, or the Implementation Guidance.

So where does that leave us? The CVE numbers alone — that +70k mark, now that Q3 is behind us — make a decent case for Vulnpocalypse, or whichever name you prefer. That part of the story is real. But discovery isn't exploitation, and that gap is exactly what the KEV numbers remind us of. Vendors seem to be keeping pace too, at least partially — KEV is growing, just not nearly at CVE's speed, which on its own would almost be good news.

Where the story breaks down is on the practical side. More than a third of actively exploited vulnerabilities still trace back to 2025 or earlier. Patch debt doesn't care how many new apocalypse-themed hashtags we invent.

So, panic? I still don't think so. Relax? Definitely not either. Somewhere between the two is where the real work sits — chipping away at that backlog, one legacy system at a time. Maybe by next quarter it'll feel less like Bugmageddon and more like business as usual. Or maybe I won't even need a warmer jacket for the upcoming "Winter of Hell."

The one big thing

Cisco Talos and Recorded Future’s Insikt Group are disclosing new espionage activity from UAT-6275 targeting government and critical infrastructure across the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). Thanks to the threat actor's own operational security lapses, researchers gained direct visibility into their infrastructure and malware development. We observed four distinct infection chains delivering custom reverse shells via macro-enabled documents, GitHub-hosted scripts, and a WinRAR vulnerability.

Why do I care?

Regional government and critical infrastructure entities are actively being targeted for diplomatic and economic intelligence. UAT-6275 is consistently evolving its tradecraft, abusing legitimate platforms like GitHub to host payloads and deploying lightweight reverse shells. Furthermore, recovered tooling suggests the group is preparing to expand its reach into Linux hosts and internet-facing appliances.

So now what?

Defenders in targeted regions and sectors should monitor for unexpected PowerShell activity and payload downloads originating from public services like GitHub. It is also critical to watch for suspicious scheduled tasks and unauthorized changes to the Windows Startup folder, which this group uses for persistence. Finally, ensure archive utilities are fully patched to prevent exploit-assisted delivery. ClamAV signatures and indicators of compromise (IOCs) to detect this threat can be found in the full blog post.

Top security headlines of the week

Hackers heat supermarket fridges to 50°C in France cyber attack The attack began overnight from Sunday to Monday. The unknown attackers reportedly abused the defrosting function in older control software, setting some equipment to heat continuously, with temperatures said to have reached 50°C. (Hack Read)

articles.title: Break the silence: Kazakhstan-nexus UAT-6275 targets CIS government organizations
articles.context: This was the first vulnerability exploit we observed in UAT-6275’s malware delivery
articles.full_text:
This research was conducted jointly with Julian-Ferdinand Vögele of Recorded Future’s Insikt Group. Details of the joint research and presentation are available here.

Cisco Talos identified UAT-6275 (TAG-193 by Recorded Future) activity targeting government organizations across the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). Recovered artifacts show additional interest in water resources and energy. This focus is consistent with intelligence collection and may reflect the regional effects of the Russia–Ukraine war.

In activity observed from June 2025 through August 2026, Talos identified four infection-chain types that use macro-enabled documents, PS2EXE downloaders, GitHub-hosted PowerShell, and a crafted WinRAR archive exploiting CVE-2025-8088. The recovered payloads include several custom reverse shells that provide interactive remote access.

Three publicly accessible staging directories and GitHub repository history exposed payload builds, tool inventories, and changes to command-and-control (C2) infrastructure. These operational security lapses gave us direct visibility into the group's recent activity.

The files recovered from the exposed infrastructure suggest preparation for post-compromise operations and potential activity against Linux hosts and internet-facing appliances.

Talos assesses with medium confidence that UAT-6275 has a Kazakhstan nexus, based on infrastructure access, language artifacts, sample submissions, working hours analysis, and regional targeting interests.

Background

Cisco Talos and Recorded Future Insikt Group jointly investigated UAT-6275 activity targeting government organizations across the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). The investigation uncovered three publicly accessible staging directories and a previously unreported GitHub repository used to host malicious scripts and payloads. These exposed assets provided visibility into the threat actor's malware development, infrastructure changes and preparations for additional intrusion activity.

Talos tracks this activity as UAT-6275, while Recorded Future tracks it as TAG-193. It overlaps with Silent Lynx (first reported by Seqrite) and sits within a broader set of campaigns connected to YoroTrooper, which we first reported in 2023. Subsequent research on Tomiris (Kaspersky), ShadowSilk (Group-IB), Cavalry Werewolf (BI.ZONE), and Hydra Saiga (VMRay) identified overlapping indicators across these reported clusters. We assess that UAT-6275 and YoroTrooper likely belong to the same broader activity cluster. However, we continue to track them separately because we have not observed direct indicator or toolset overlap between the two.

This post summarizes our joint Virus Bulletin 2026 white paper, “Break the silence: tracking Silent Lynx through exposed infrastructure” which contains the full technical analysis and indicators of compromise (IOCs).

Victimology

UAT-6275's targeting is concentrated in Central Asia and the wider CIS region. Across the reviewed campaigns, observed victims and lure themes span nine countries: Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Russia, and Belarus.

Figure 1. Regional targeting.

Government and diplomatic affairs

UAT-6275 targets government institutions responsible for diplomacy, economic development, agriculture, and environmental management. These organizations hold information that can inform bilateral negotiations, economic planning, and regional security decisions.

Our network flow analysis identified activity involving a Tajik government entity shortly after treaty discussions with Kazakhstan in March 2026 and a Belarusian government entity ahead of a bilateral meeting in April. This timing may indicate an interest in regional diplomatic developments.

The decoy documents we recovered also suggest an interest in diplomatic relations, international trade, and aviation. Examples include a diplomatic letter addressed to Armenia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Figure 2. Lure document masquerading as a Russian diplomatic congratulatory letter to the Armenian Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Water security and resource management

The group’s interest in regional resources spans environmental management and energy. Talos observed activity involving an Armenian government entity responsible for environmental matters and Uzbekistan’s Smart Forestry initiative, consistent with earlier reporting on Silent Lynx targeting water resource organizations across Central Asia.

Energy-themed decoys included a cooperation proposal between Turkmenistan’s state oil company, Turkmennebit, and Russia’s Orsk Oil Refinery, used in an August 2025 sample. The refinery supplies petroleum products to Kazakhstan and later shut down after a Ukrainian drone strike in August 2026, with repairs expected to take up to six months. These ties suggest a possible intelligence interest in regional fuel supplies and the war’s implications for Kazakhstan’s energy security.

Figure 3. Decoy impersonating Turkmennebit and proposing cooperation with Orsk Oil Refinery management.

Campaign timeline

Since Seqrite first reported Silent Lynx in January 2025, we have identified at least eight campaigns across the region through May 2026. These include malware delivery targeting Russia, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan; a credential-harvesting site impersonating Azerbaijan’s State Agency for Public Service; and lures referencing the China–Central Asia Summit and Russian energy infrastructure. In 2026, we also observed activity involving government entities in Tajikistan, Armenia, and Belarus, as well as Uzbekistan’s Smart Forestry initiative in May.

Figure 4. Campaign timeline.

Infrastructure and malware delivery

Talos identified three publicly accessible staging directories containing malware and tools of UAT-6275. One sample led to the previously unreported GitHub repository, where the group hosted PowerShell scripts and payloads. Its commit history allowed us to track infrastructure changes and malware development.

The group relies on lightweight reverse shells, including Chvost, Laplas, and PickleShell, to issue commands on compromised systems.

We also recovered Linux-compatible tooling and a publicly available proof-of-concept exploit for FortiWeb CVE-2025-25257 from UAT-6275 infrastructure. These findings suggest interest in expanding the group’s operational capabilities.

Four infection chains

UAT-6275 used malicious documents, executable downloaders, and shortcuts to deliver malware, and later incorporated a WinRAR exploit. Talos categorized the recovered samples into four infection chains, A – D, based on how they retrieve and execute their payloads.

Figure 5. First observations of four UAT-6275 infection chains, June 2025 – April 2026.

The first Chain A samples, observed in June 2025, used macro-enabled Word documents to download and execute a second-stage binary. In July 2025, we observed Chain B downloaders built with PS2EXE, a tool that packages PowerShell scripts as standalone Windows executables. These downloaders retrieved reverse-shell payloads and created scheduled tasks for persistence.

We first observed Chain C in October 2025. A malicious shortcut launches PowerShell to retrieve and execute a GitHub-hosted script that provides remote shell access. Later samples also downloaded PickleShell and placed it in the Windows Startup folder for persistence.

Figure 6. Chain C retrieves a GitHub-hosted PowerShell script; later samples also deploy PickleShell to the Startup folder.

In April 2026, we identified a RAR archive that exploited CVE-2025-8088 in WinRAR to place PickleShell in the Windows Startup folder (Chain D). The payload runs at the next user sign-in. This was the first vulnerability exploit we observed in UAT-6275’s malware delivery.

Figure 7. Chain D exploits CVE-2025-8088 to place PickleShell in the Windows Startup folder for execution at the next sign-in.

Kazakhstan nexus assessment

Talos assesses with medium confidence that UAT-6275 has a Kazakhstan nexus. Supporting evidence includes Russian-language artifacts, apparent malware-testing submissions from Kazakhstan shortly after compilation, and operator activity consistent with UTC+5 working hours.

Figure 8. Timing of 77 GitHub commits in UTC+3 and UTC+5, with 09:00–18:00 local working hours shaded.

Looking ahead

UAT-6275’s sustained activity and adoption of new delivery techniques suggest the group will continue pursuing access to government organizations across Central Asia and the CIS. Its interest in environmental agencies, economic ministries, and energy infrastructure reflects the intelligence value of regional diplomacy and resource management.

Defenders in these sectors should monitor unexpected PowerShell activity and payload downloads from public services such as GitHub, alongside scheduled tasks and Startup-folder changes. Keeping archive utilities patched can help reduce exposure to the exploit-assisted delivery observed in this campaign.

For further details on this research and our accompanying presentation, see “Break the Silence: Tracking Silent Lynx Through Exposed Infrastructure” on Virus Bulletin’s website, as well as Recorded Future’s related blog post.
